metadata.title: Unexpected hypersurfaces and where to find them

extraction_notes.note: Theorem 1.2 (mainThm) restates Theorem 2.15 (both numbered environments, same content); kept Theorem 2.15, which carries the proof, and emitted no node for Theorem 1.2. Its only \ref is in introductory prose that is not a node.

Open problem 6 of Section 5 repeats Question 2.11 word for word and gets no node. Table 1 (B_{n+1} cases), the TikZ figures, the B_4 base-locus computation recipe and the script-efficiency variants (alternative verbatim blocks, random-point variant) are not separate nodes.

The proof of Corollary 2.20 hard-codes 'Proposition 2.4' and 'the proof of Corollary 2.16'; 2.16 is a Definition, so it was read as the proof of Corollary 2.18 (WLP for curves in P^3) and linked at confidence 0.6.
Proposition 2.17 is presented as 'we get', but the paper says it is equivalent to a special case of [DI, Theorem 13], so it is marked external with the paper's own direct proof.

The Macaulay2 'universal script' sits in a verbatim block, not a pseudocode environment; it was extracted as an unmarked algorithm whose steps are spans of code lines; the outermost loop over n spans the whole script, so it is not a separate step (it would be the single child of the algorithm) and its body lines are direct children.
Results of computer searches over root systems are stated as findings in prose; extracted as claims with rigor numerical rather than as examples or remarks.
Conjectures taken from hedged prose ('It seems likely', 'Examples suggest'); CnjP2 includes the two set-up sentences that define Z, C and F so the statement stands alone.

nodes.name: Unexpected plane curve
nodes.statement: Given a finite set of points $Z\subset\ensuremath{\mathbb{P}}^n$ with $n=2$, we say that plane curves of degree $d=m+1$ containing $Z$ and having a general point of multiplicity $m$ are {\it unexpected} when such curves exist but the conditions imposed by vanishing to order $m$ at $P$ on the vector space of forms of degree $d$ vanishing on $Z$ are not independent.
nodes.genus: plane curves of degree $d=m+1$ containing $Z$ and having a general point of multiplicity $m$
nodes.statement_short: Plane curves of degree m+1 through Z with a general m-fold point are unexpected when they exist but the fat point imposes dependent conditions.

nodes.name: Ground field K
nodes.statement: To describe the problem and our approach to it in a more precise way, let $\ensuremath{\mathbb{K}}$ be an algebraically closed field of characteristic 0.

nodes.name: Homogeneous coordinate ring R
nodes.statement: Let $R=\ensuremath{\mathbb{K}}[\ensuremath{\mathbb{P}}^n]=\ensuremath{\mathbb{K}}[x_0,\ldots,x_n]$ be the homogeneous coordinate ring of $n$-dimensional projective space.

nodes.name: Fat point scheme
nodes.statement: Consider a general point $P\in\ensuremath{\mathbb{P}}^n$. The fat point scheme $X=mP$ is the scheme defined by the homogeneous ideal $I_X=(I_{P})^{m} \subset R$, where $I_{P}$ is the ideal generated by all forms that vanish at $P$.

nodes.name: Degree-d component [I]_d
nodes.statement: Given a homogeneous ideal $I\subseteq R$, we denote by $[I]_d$ the $\ensuremath{\mathbb{K}}$-vector space spanned by homogeneous forms in $I$ of degree $d$.

nodes.name: Dimension of forms vanishing on a fat point
nodes.statement: It is well known and easy to show that $\dim_\ensuremath{\mathbb{K}}[I_X]_d=\max(0,\binom{n+d}{n}-\binom{m-1+n}{n})$.
conclusions: $\dim_\ensuremath{\mathbb{K}}[I_X]_d=\max(0,\binom{n+d}{n}-\binom{m-1+n}{n})$
nodes.statement_short: An m-fold point imposes independent conditions on degree-d forms.

nodes.name: Reduced point scheme Z
nodes.statement: Given distinct points $Q_i\in\ensuremath{\mathbb{P}}^n$, we define $Z=Q_1+\cdots +Q_s$ to be the subscheme defined by the ideal $I_Z=\cap_jI_{Q_j}\subset R$.

nodes.name: Unexpected hypersurface
nodes.statement: We say that $Z\subset\ensuremath{\mathbb{P}}^n$ {\em admits an unexpected hypersurface} with respect to $X$ of degree $d$ if $$\dim [I_Z\cap I_X]_d > \max \left \{ 0, \dim [I_Z]_d-\binom{m-1+n}{n} \right \}.$$ That is, $Z$ admits an unexpected hypersurface with respect to $X$ of degree $d$ if the conditions imposed by $X$ on forms of degree $d$ vanishing on $Z$ are not independent. We will also sometimes say that $Z$ admits an unexpected hypersurface with a general point $P$ of multiplicity~$m$.
differentia: the conditions imposed by $X$ on forms of degree $d$ vanishing on $Z$ are not independent
nodes.statement_short: Z admits an unexpected hypersurface of degree d w.r.t. X=mP if dim[I_Z∩I_X]_d exceeds max{0, dim[I_Z]_d - binom(m-1+n,n)}.

nodes.name: Classification of unexpected hypersurfaces
nodes.statement: Characterize and then classify all quadruples $(n,d,m,Z)$ where $Z\subset\ensuremath{\mathbb{P}}^n$ admits an unexpected hypersurface of degree $d$ with a general point $P$ of multiplicity $m$.
nodes.statement_short: Classify all (n,d,m,Z) for which Z admits an unexpected hypersurface of degree d with a general m-fold point.
nodes.label: prob:intro

nodes.name: Saturated ideal and ideal sheaf notation
nodes.statement: For any subvariety (or subscheme) $V \subseteq \ensuremath{\mathbb{P}}^n$ we write $I_V \subseteq R$ for the saturated ideal of $V$ and $\mathcal{I}_V$ for the sheaf on $\ensuremath{\mathbb{P}}^n$ corresponding to $I_V$.

nodes.name: First difference of a function
nodes.statement: For any integer function $h : \ensuremath{\mathbb{Z}}_{\geq 0} \to \ensuremath{\mathbb{Z}}$ the first difference $\Delta h$ is the backward difference $\Delta h(t) = h(t)-h(t-1)$, where we make the convention $h(-1)=0$ (so $\Delta h(0) = h(0)$).

nodes.name: Cone with vertex P
nodes.statement: By a cone with vertex $P$ we mean a scheme $X$ such that for every point $Q$ in $X$ the line joining $P$ and $Q$ is in $X$.
differentia: for every point $Q$ in $X$ the line joining $P$ and $Q$ is in $X$

nodes.name: Maximal multiplicity hypersurfaces are cones
nodes.statement: In particular, by B\'ezout, every hypersurface of degree $d$ with a point of multiplicity $d$ at a point $P$ is a cone with vertex $P$.
assumptions: every hypersurface of degree $d$ with a point of multiplicity $d$ at a point $P$
conclusions: is a cone with vertex $P$

nodes.name: Plane curves in P^3 admit no unexpected cone
nodes.statement: It is not hard to show that a plane curve of degree $d$ in $\ensuremath{\mathbb{P}}^3$ does not admit an unexpected hypersurface with a point of multiplicity $d$ -- instead, a point of multiplicity $d$ imposes the expected number of conditions on hypersurfaces of degree $d$ containing the plane curve (use the fact that a plane curve in $\ensuremath{\mathbb{P}}^3$ is a complete intersection, and the known Hilbert function for complete intersections).
assumptions: a plane curve of degree $d$ in $\ensuremath{\mathbb{P}}^3$
conclusions: does not admit an unexpected hypersurface with a point of multiplicity $d$
nodes.statement_short: A degree-d plane curve in P^3 imposes the expected conditions with a d-fold general point (complete intersection).

nodes.name: Cone over a non-degenerate space curve is unexpected
nodes.statement: Let $C$ be a reduced, equidimensional, non-degenerate curve of degree $d$ in $\ensuremath{\mathbb{P}}^3$ ($C$ may be reducible, disconnected, and/or singular but note that $d \geq 2$ since $C$ is non-degenerate, with $C$ being two skew lines if $d=2$). Let $P \in \ensuremath{\mathbb{P}}^3$ be a general point. Then the cone $S_P=S_P(C)$ over $C$ with vertex $P$ is an unexpected surface of degree $d$ for $C$ with multiplicity $d$ at $P$. It is the unique unexpected surface of this degree and multiplicity.
assumptions: Let $C$ be a reduced, equidimensional, non-degenerate curve of degree $d$ in $\ensuremath{\mathbb{P}}^3$
Let $P \in \ensuremath{\mathbb{P}}^3$ be a general point.
conclusions: Then the cone $S_P=S_P(C)$ over $C$ with vertex $P$ is an unexpected surface of degree $d$ for $C$ with multiplicity $d$ at $P$.
It is the unique unexpected surface of this degree and multiplicity.
nodes.statement_short: For a non-degenerate space curve C of degree d, the cone over C from a general point is the unique unexpected degree-d surface with a d-fold point.
nodes.label: cone in P3

nodes.name: Proof of Proposition 2.1
nodes.statement:
We first check uniqueness. Let $F$ be a form defining a surface containing $C$, of degree $d$ with multiplicity $d$ at $P$. Let $\lambda$ be a line through $P$ and any point $Q$, of $C$. Then by B'ezout, $F$ must vanish on all of $\lambda$. Thus the surface defined by $F$ is precisely $S_P$. We now check unexpectedness. Let $D$ be a smooth plane curve of degree $d$. \medskip 
oindent \underline{Claim 1}: {\em The arithmetic genus, $g_C$, of $C$ is strictly less than that of $D$, which is $g_D =  inom{d-1}{2}$. } \medskip This argument is classical. Much of it is given in \cite{harris} (when C is irreducible) and in \cite{migbook} Proposition 1.4.2, so no claim is made to originality; we include it here just for the reader's convenience. Let $\Gamma$ be a general hyperplane section of $C$ by a hyperplane $H$ defined by a general linear form $L$. Let $I_{\Gamma | H}$ be the saturated ideal of $\Gamma$ in $H$. Let $\ell \gg 0$. Then \[  egin{array}{rcl} d\ell - g_C + 1 & = & h^0(\mathcal O_C(\ell)) \ & = & h_{R/I_C}(\ell) \end{array} \] where $h_{R/I_C}(t)$ is the Hilbert function of $C$. On the other hand, for any integer $t$ we have the exact sequence \[  egin{array}{ccccccccccccccccccc} 0 & ightarrow & [I_C]_{t-1} & ightarrow & [I_C]_t & ightarrow & [I_{\Gamma|H} ]_t & \longrightarrow & H^1(\mathcal I_C(t-1)) & ightarrow & \dots \ &&&&&&\hbox{\ \ \ \ \ \ \ } \searrow & & 
earrow \hbox{\ \ \ \ \ \ \ \ \ \ \ \ } \ &&&&&&& [K]_t \ &&&&&&\hbox{\ \ \ \ \ \ \ } 
earrow & & \searrow \hbox{\ \ \ \ \ \ \ \ \ \ \ \ } \ &&&&&&\hbox{\ } 0 & & 0 \hbox{\ \ \ \ \ \ } \ \end{array} \] (where $K$ is just the cokernel). Then after adding and subtracting some binomial coefficients and setting $ ar R = R/L$, we obtain \[  egin{array}{rcl} \Delta h_{R/I_C} (t) & = & h_{ ar R/I_{\Gamma|H}}(t) + \dim [K]_t \ & \geq & h_{ ar R/I_{\Gamma | H}} (t). \end{array} \] So since $\ell \gg 0$ we obtain \[  egin{array}{rcl} g_C & = & 1 + d\ell - h_{R/I_C}(\ell) \ & = & d\ell - \sum_{t=1}^\ell \Delta h_{R/I_C}(t) \ & \leq & d\ell - \sum_{t=1}^\ell h_{ ar R/I_{\Gamma|H}} (t) \ & = & \sum_{t=1}^\ell \left [ d - h_{ ar R/I_{\Gamma | H}} (t) ight ]. \end{array} \] Now replace $C$ by $D$, and replace $\Gamma$ by the hyperplane section of $D$, which is a set of $d$ collinear points, say $A$. We have, similarly, \[ g_D = \sum_{t=1}^\ell \left [ d - h_{ ar R/I_A}(t) ight ] =  inom{d-1}{2} . \] It is clear that for any $t \geq 1$ we have \[ h_{ ar R/I_{\Gamma|H}} (t) \geq h_{ ar R/I_A}(t) \] with strict inequality for $t=1$, so we obtain $g_C < g_D$. This completes the proof of Claim 1. Now, by \cite{GLP} Remark (1) (p. 497), we have $H^1(\mathcal I_C(d)) = H^2(\mathcal I_C(d)) = 0$, and we also have $H^1(\mathcal I_D(d)) = H^2(\mathcal I_D(d)) = 0$. Consider the exact sequence \[ 0 ightarrow [I_C]_d ightarrow H^0(\mathcal O_{\ensuremath{\mathbb{P}}^3}(d)) ightarrow H^0(\mathcal O_C(d)) ightarrow H^1(\mathcal I_C(d)) ightarrow 0. \] \medskip 
oindent \underline{Claim 2}: {\em Let $D$ be a plane curve of degree $d$. Then $h^0(\mathcal O_C(d)) > h^0(\mathcal O_D(d))$.} \medskip Indeed, \[  egin{array}{rcl} d^2 - g_C + 1 & = & h^0(\mathcal O_C(d)) - h^1(\mathcal O_C(d)) \ & = & h^0(\mathcal O_C(d)) - h^2(\mathcal I_C(d)) \ & = & h^0(\mathcal O_C(d)) \end{array} \] and similarly for $D$, so thanks to Claim 1 we have \[ h^0(\mathcal O_C(d)) > h^0(\mathcal O_D(d)) \] and we have Claim 2. Then \[  egin{array}{rcll} \dim [I_C]_d & = & \displaystyle  inom{d+3}{3} - h^0(\mathcal O_C(d)) & \hbox{(since } h^1(\mathcal I_C(d)) = 0 ) \ \ & < & \displaystyle  inom{d+3}{3} - h^0(\mathcal O_D(d)) \end{array} \] thanks to Claim 2. To check that $S_P$ is an unexpected surface it is enough to note that \[  egin{array}{rcl} \displaystyle \dim [I_C]_d -  inom{d-1+3}{3} & < & \displaystyle  inom{d+3}{3} - h^0(\mathcal O_D(d)) -  inom{d-1+3}{3} \ \ & = & \displaystyle  inom{d+2}{2} - [d^2 - g_D + 1] \ \ & = & 1 \end{array} \] using the value of $g_D$ mentioned above.
nodes.statement_short: Uniqueness by Bezout; unexpectedness by comparing Hilbert functions with a plane curve. Key step: the genus bound g_C < g_D (Claim 1) via hyperplane sections, giving h^0(O_C(d)) > h^0(O_D(d)).

nodes.name: No low-degree cones through codimension two varieties
nodes.statement: The same argument that was used to show uniqueness in the last result also shows that if $C$ is a curve of degree $d$ in $\ensuremath{\mathbb{P}}^3$ then there does not exist a surface of degree $e \leq d-1$ containing $C$ with a singularity of multiplicty $e$ at a general point, since B\'ezout would force $S_P$ to be a component of such a surface. This means that $\dim [I_C]_e \leq \binom{(e-1)+3}{3}$ for all $1 \leq e \leq d$ (where the statement for degree $d$ is given in the proof). In fact, the same argument works for a subvariety $V$ of $\ensuremath{\mathbb{P}}^n$ of codimension two and degree $d$, to show that $\dim [I_V]_e \leq \binom{(e-1)+n}{n}$ for $1 \leq e \leq d-1$. This statement also extends to the case $e=d$, and the argument is contained in the proof of Proposition \ref{Pn}.
nodes.statement_short: By Bezout, no surface of degree e<d through C has an e-fold general point, so dim[I_C]_e <= binom(e-1+3,3); likewise in codimension 2 in P^n.
nodes.label: low deg rmk

nodes.name: Hyperplane sections stay non-degenerate
nodes.statement: Let $V$ be a reduced, equidimensional, non-degenerate subvariety of $\ensuremath{\mathbb{P}}^n$ ($n \geq 4$) of codimension 2 (not necessarily irreducible). Let $H$ be a general hyperplane and let $W = V \cap H$. Then $W$ is non-degenerate in $H = \ensuremath{\mathbb{P}}^{n-1}$.
assumptions: Let $V$ be a reduced, equidimensional, non-degenerate subvariety of $\ensuremath{\mathbb{P}}^n$ ($n \geq 4$) of codimension 2 (not necessarily irreducible).
Let $H$ be a general hyperplane and let $W = V \cap H$.
conclusions: Then $W$ is non-degenerate in $H = \ensuremath{\mathbb{P}}^{n-1}$.
nodes.label: nondeg

nodes.name: Proof of Lemma 2.3
nodes.statement: We have the exact sequence \[ 0 \rightarrow [I_V]_0 \rightarrow [I_V]_1 \rightarrow [I_{W|H}]_1 \rightarrow H^1(\mathcal I_V (0)) \rightarrow \dots \] We want to show that the third vector space in this exact sequence is zero. But $[I_V]_1 = 0$ since $V$ is non-degenerate. On the other hand, we claim that $H^1(\mathcal I_V(0)) = 0$. This will complete the proof. But we also have the exact sequence \[ 0 \rightarrow [I_V]_0 \rightarrow [R]_0 \rightarrow H^0(\mathcal O_V(0)) \rightarrow H^1(\mathcal I_V(0)) \rightarrow 0. \] The first term is clearly zero. The second has dimension 1. The third has dimension 1 since $V$ is connected (being of codimension 2 and equidimensional) and reduced (by hypothesis). Thus the claim follows.
nodes.statement_short: Restriction exact sequence; vanishing of H^1(I_V(0)) since V is connected and reduced.

nodes.name: Cone over a codimension two subvariety is unexpected
nodes.statement: Let $V$ be a reduced, equidimensional, non-degenerate subvariety of $\ensuremath{\mathbb{P}}^n$ ($n \geq 3$) of codimension 2 and degree $d$ ($V$ may be reducible and/or singular but note that $d \geq 2$ since $V$ is non-degenerate, with $V$ being two codimension 2 linear spaces if $d=2$). Let $P \in \ensuremath{\mathbb{P}}^n$ be a general point. Then the cone $S_P$ over $V$ with vertex $P$ is an unexpected hypersurface for $V$ of degree $d$ and multiplicity $d$ at $P$. It is the unique unexpected hypersurface of this degree and multiplicity.
assumptions: Let $V$ be a reduced, equidimensional, non-degenerate subvariety of $\ensuremath{\mathbb{P}}^n$ ($n \geq 3$) of codimension 2 and degree $d$
Let $P \in \ensuremath{\mathbb{P}}^n$ be a general point.
conclusions: Then the cone $S_P$ over $V$ with vertex $P$ is an unexpected hypersurface for $V$ of degree $d$ and multiplicity $d$ at $P$.
nodes.statement_short: Cones over non-degenerate codimension-2 subvarieties of degree d give unique unexpected degree-d hypersurfaces with a d-fold general point.
nodes.label: Pn

nodes.name: Proof of Proposition 2.4
nodes.statement: The proof is by induction on $n$. The initial case is Proposition \ref{cone in P3}, so we can assume $n \geq 4$. Let $H$ be a general hyperplane through $P$ and let $W = V \cap H$. Since $P$ is general, we can assume that $H$ is general as well. By Lemma \ref{nondeg}, $W$ is non-degenerate in $H = \ensuremath{\mathbb{P}}^{n-1}$, and it is also reduced and equidimensional. Let $T_P$ be the cone in $H$ over $W$ with vertex $P$. Thus by induction, $T_P$ is the unique hypersurface of degree $d$ containing $W$ with multiplicity $d$ at $P$, and it is unexpected. Consider the exact sequence \[ \begin{array}{ccccccccccccccccccc} 0 & \rightarrow & [I_V]_{d-1} & \rightarrow & [I_V]_d & \rightarrow & [I_{W|H} ]_d & \longrightarrow & H^1(\mathcal I_V(d-1)) & \rightarrow & \dots \\ &&&&&&\hbox{\ \ \ \ \ \ \ } \searrow & & \nearrow \hbox{\ \ \ \ \ \ \ \ \ \ \ \ } \\ &&&&&&& [K]_d \\ &&&&&&\hbox{\ \ \ \ \ \ \ } \nearrow & & \searrow \hbox{\ \ \ \ \ \ \ \ \ \ \ \ } \\ &&&&&&\hbox{\ } 0 & & 0 \hbox{\ \ \ \ \ \ } \\ \end{array} \] We have \[ \dim [I_V]_d = \dim [I_V]_{d-1} + \dim [I_{W|H}]_d - \dim [K]_d. \] We claim that \[ \dim [I_V]_d - \binom{d-1+n}{n} \leq 0 \] so that $S_P$ is unexpected. We have \[ \begin{array}{rcl} \displaystyle \dim [I_V]_d - \binom{d-1+n}{n} & = & \displaystyle \dim [I_V]_{d-1} + \left ( \dim [I_{W|H}]_d - \binom{d-1+(n-1)}{n-1} \right ) \\ \\ && \displaystyle + \binom{d-1+(n-1)}{n-1} - \dim [K]_d - \binom{d-1+n}{n} \\ \\ & \leq & \displaystyle \dim [I_V]_{d-1} + \binom{d+n-2}{n-1} - \dim [K]_d - \binom{d+n-1}{n} \\ \\ & = & \displaystyle \dim [I_V]_{d-1} - \binom{d+n-2}{n} - \dim [K]_d . \end{array} \] But Remark \ref{low deg rmk} gives \[ \dim [I_V]_{d-1} \leq \binom{d+n-2}{n}, \] which completes the claim. Uniqueness follows in the same way as it did for Proposition~\ref{cone in P3}.
nodes.statement_short: Induction on n via a general hyperplane section through P, with Lemma 2.3 and the bound of Remark 2.2.

nodes.name: Unexpected cones for points on a space curve
nodes.statement: Let $C$ be a reduced, equidimensional, non-degenerate curve of degree $d$ in $\ensuremath{\mathbb{P}}^3$ ($C$ may be reducible, singular, and/or disconnected). Let $P \in \ensuremath{\mathbb{P}}^3$ be a general point. Let $Z \subset C$ be any set of points on $C$ such that $[I_C]_d = [I_Z]_d$. Then the cone $S_P$ over $C$ with vertex $P$ is an unexpected surface of degree $d$ for $Z$ with multiplicity $d$ at $P$. It is the unique unexpected surface of this degree and multiplicity. In particular, we may choose $Z$ to impose independent conditions on forms of degree $d$.
assumptions: Let $C$ be a reduced, equidimensional, non-degenerate curve of degree $d$ in $\ensuremath{\mathbb{P}}^3$
Let $P \in \ensuremath{\mathbb{P}}^3$ be a general point.
Let $Z \subset C$ be any set of points on $C$ such that $[I_C]_d = [I_Z]_d$.
conclusions: Then the cone $S_P$ over $C$ with vertex $P$ is an unexpected surface of degree $d$ for $Z$ with multiplicity $d$ at $P$.
nodes.statement_short: Points on a non-degenerate space curve with the same degree-d forms as the curve inherit the unexpected cone.
nodes.label: curves 1

nodes.name: Proof of Corollary 2.5
nodes.statement: It is immediate from the hypothesis that $[I_C]_d = [I_Z]_d$.
nodes.statement_short: Immediate from [I_C]_d = [I_Z]_d and Proposition 2.1.

nodes.name: Unexpected cones for many points on a smooth space curve
nodes.statement: Let $C$ be a smooth, irreducible, non-degenerate curve of degree $d \geq 3$ in $\ensuremath{\mathbb{P}}^3$. Let $P \in \ensuremath{\mathbb{P}}^3$ be a general point. Let $Z \subset C$ be any set of at least $d^2+1$ points on $C$ (general or not). Then the cone $S_P$ over $C$ with vertex $P$ is an unexpected surface of degree $d$ for $Z$ with multiplicity $d$ at $P$. It is the unique unexpected surface of this degree and multiplicity.
assumptions: Let $C$ be a smooth, irreducible, non-degenerate curve of degree $d \geq 3$ in $\ensuremath{\mathbb{P}}^3$.
Let $Z \subset C$ be any set of at least $d^2+1$ points on $C$ (general or not).
conclusions: Then the cone $S_P$ over $C$ with vertex $P$ is an unexpected surface of degree $d$ for $Z$ with multiplicity $d$ at $P$.
nodes.label: curves 2

nodes.name: Ten points on a twisted cubic
nodes.statement: Let $C$ be a twisted cubic curve in $\ensuremath{\mathbb{P}}^3$. Then $d=3$ and $g_C = 0$. Let $Z$ be a set of $10$ points on $C$, so $[I_C]_3 = [I_Z]_3$ has dimension $10$. In this case $\dim [I_Z]_3 - \binom{2+3}{3} = 10 - 10 = 0$ so we do not expect a hypersurface of degree 3 with multiplicity 3 at a general point containing the 10 points of $Z$. But in fact there is such an unexpected hypersurface, given by the cone over $C$ with vertex at a general point.
nodes.statement_short: Ten points on a twisted cubic: expected dimension 0, yet the cone over the cubic is an unexpected cubic surface.
nodes.label: twc1

nodes.name: Fewer points suffice
nodes.statement: Corollary \ref{curves 1}, Corollary \ref{curves 2}, Corollary \ref{add S} and Corollary \ref{WLP Pn cons} all deal with the situation that we begin with a set of points lying on a variety $C$ of codimension two in $\ensuremath{\mathbb{P}}^n$, and have enough points so that $[I_C]_d = [I_Z]_d$. In fact this assumption can be relaxed, although the statement becomes a little bit less transparent so we retained this assumption. But notice that the fact that $C$ already admits an unexpected hypersurface of degree $d$ means that we only need a set of $\binom{d+n}{n} - \binom{d-1+n}{n}$ points on $C$ that impose independent conditions on forms of degree $d$, and this number can be much smaller than the number forced by the condition $[I_C]_d = [I_Z]_d$. For example, say $C$ is a general smooth rational curve in $\ensuremath{\mathbb{P}}^3$ of degree 6. The Hilbert function of $C$ is given by the sequence $1,4,10, 19, 25, 31, 37, \dots$ so the assumption that $[I_C]_6 = [I_Z]_6$ means we need $Z$ to have at least 37 points of $C$. Instead, suppose that $Z$ is a sufficiently general set of $\binom{6+3}{3} - \binom{5+3}{3} = 28$ points on $C$. Then the Hilbert function of $Z$ is given by the sequence $1,4,10,19, 25, 28, 28, \dots$ and we still do not expect a hypersurface of degree 6 with a point of multiplicity 6 to contain $Z$, but we know that the cone over $C$ is such a hypersurface. Notice that in this case we not only have $[I_C]_6 \neq [I_Z]_6$ but even $[I_C]_5 \neq [I_Z]_5$.
nodes.statement_short: Only binom(d+n,n)-binom(d-1+n,n) independent points on C are needed; e.g. 28 instead of 37 points on a rational sextic.
nodes.label: need fewer pts

nodes.name: Unexpected cones for points on a union of lines
nodes.statement: Let $C$ be a non-degenerate union of $d$ lines in $\ensuremath{\mathbb{P}}^3$. Let $P \in \ensuremath{\mathbb{P}}^3$ be a general point. Let $Z \subset C$ be a set of $d(d+1)$ points on $C$ chosen by taking $d+1$ general points on each line. Then the cone $S_P$ over $C$ with vertex $P$ is an unexpected surface of degree $d$ for $Z$ with multiplicity $d$ at $P$. It is the unique unexpected surface of this degree and multiplicity.
assumptions: Let $C$ be a non-degenerate union of $d$ lines in $\ensuremath{\mathbb{P}}^3$.
Let $Z \subset C$ be a set of $d(d+1)$ points on $C$ chosen by taking $d+1$ general points on each line.
conclusions: Then the cone $S_P$ over $C$ with vertex $P$ is an unexpected surface of degree $d$ for $Z$ with multiplicity $d$ at $P$.

nodes.name: General points admit no unexpected hypersurface
nodes.statement: On the other hand, it is not the case that all sets of points in $\ensuremath{\mathbb{P}}^3$ (or any other projective space) admit an unexpected surface (resp. hypersurface) of some sort. Indeed, suppose $Z$ is a general set of points in $\ensuremath{\mathbb{P}}^3$ and let us ask if there is any degree and multiplicity at a general point, in which $Z$ admits an unexpected surface. By considering the conditions imposed first by the general multiple point and then by the general points $Z$, we see that we must always get the expected number of conditions. What is interesting is that in \cite{CHMN} Corollary 6.8 it was shown that a set of points in linear general position in $\ensuremath{\mathbb{P}}^2$ does not admit an unexpected curve of degree $d$ and multiplicity $d-1$ at a general point. Example \ref{twc1} already shows that this does not extend to a set of points in linear general position in $\ensuremath{\mathbb{P}}^3$, if we weaken the condition on the multiplicity to allow multiplicity $d$. We do not know if the precise result from \cite{CHMN} continues to hold in higher dimensional projective spaces.
nodes.statement_short: General points never admit unexpected hypersurfaces; CHMN's linear-general-position result in P^2 fails in P^3 for multiplicity d.
nodes.label: no unexp for genl pts

nodes.name: No unexpected curves for points in linear general position (CHMN Corollary 6.8)
nodes.statement: What is interesting is that in \cite{CHMN} Corollary 6.8 it was shown that a set of points in linear general position in $\ensuremath{\mathbb{P}}^2$ does not admit an unexpected curve of degree $d$ and multiplicity $d-1$ at a general point.
assumptions: a set of points in linear general position in $\ensuremath{\mathbb{P}}^2$
conclusions: does not admit an unexpected curve of degree $d$ and multiplicity $d-1$ at a general point

nodes.name: Unexpected hypersurfaces for points in linear general position
nodes.statement: Let $Z$ be a non-degenerate set of points in linear general position in $\ensuremath{\mathbb{P}}^n$, $n \geq 3$. Is it true that there does not exist an unexpected hypersurface of any degree $d$ and multiplicity $d-1$ at a general point?
nodes.statement_short: Do points in linear general position in P^n (n>=3) never admit an unexpected hypersurface of degree d with a (d-1)-fold general point?
nodes.label: GLPQ

nodes.name: Unexpected cones of higher degree
nodes.statement: Let $C$ be a reduced, equidimensional, non-degenerate curve of degree $d \geq 2$ in $\ensuremath{\mathbb{P}}^3$ ($C$ may be reducible, singular, and/or disconnected). Let $P \in \ensuremath{\mathbb{P}}^3$ be a general point. Let $k \geq d$ be a positive integer. Then $C$ admits an unexpected surface of degree $k$ with multiplicity $k$ at $P$.
assumptions: Let $C$ be a reduced, equidimensional, non-degenerate curve of degree $d \geq 2$ in $\ensuremath{\mathbb{P}}^3$
Let $P \in \ensuremath{\mathbb{P}}^3$ be a general point.
Let $k \geq d$ be a positive integer.
conclusions: Then $C$ admits an unexpected surface of degree $k$ with multiplicity $k$ at $P$.
nodes.label: higher deg

nodes.name: Proof of Corollary 2.12
nodes.statement: Let $Y = C \cup kP$. We want to show that \begin{equation} \max \left\{ 0 , \dim[I_C]_k - \binom{k+2}{3} \right\} < \dim [I_Y]_k. \end{equation} Modifying the calculation above, we know that \[ \dim [I_C]_k = \binom{k+3}{3} - [dk - g_C + 1] \] so \[ \dim [I_C]_k - \binom{k+2}{3} = \binom{k+2}{2} - dk + g_C -1. \] On the other hand, we have a unique surface $S_P$ of degree $d$ with a singularity of multiplicity $d$ at the general point $P$, so by multiplying $S_P$ by an element of $[I_P^{k-d}]_{k-d}$ we always obtain a surface of degree $k$ with multiplicity $k$ at $P$. Thus \[ \dim [I_Y]_k \geq \binom{k-d+2}{2}, \] in particular $\dim [I_Y]_k > 0$. Thus combining, it is enough to show \[ \binom{k+2}{2} - dk + g_C -1 < \binom{k-d+2}{2}. \] A calculation shows that this is equivalent to \[ g_C < \frac{(d-1)(d-2)}{2}, \] which we showed in Claim 1 of Proposition \ref{cone in P3}.
nodes.statement_short: Multiply the cone S_P by forms in I_P^{k-d} to bound dim[I_Y]_k from below; reduce to the genus bound of Claim 1 in Proposition 2.1.

nodes.name: Inequality to show for higher-degree cones
nodes.statement: \max \left\{ 0 , \dim[I_C]_k - \binom{k+2}{3} \right\} < \dim [I_Y]_k.
nodes.label: to show

nodes.name: Analogous corollaries in higher degree
nodes.statement: Although we do not state them explicitly, we get the analogous corollaries for ``sufficiently many" points on $C$ that we got for Proposition \ref{cone in P3}, but now in higher degree. The key is to assume (directly or by a condition on the number of points) that $[I_C]_k = [I_Z]_k$.

nodes.name: Unexpected hypersurfaces with multiplicity less than degree
nodes.statement: Let $V$ be a reduced, equidimensional, non-degenerate subvariety of codimension two and degree $d$ in $\ensuremath{\mathbb{P}}^n$, $n \geq 3$. Let $S$ be a hypersurface of degree $e \geq 1$ not containing any irreducible component of $V$. Let $Y = V \cup S$. Let $Z \subset Y$ be a finite set of points such that $[I_Z]_{d+e} = [I_Y]_{d+e}$. Let $P$ be a general point in $\ensuremath{\mathbb{P}}^n$. Then $Z$ admits a unique unexpected hypersurface of degree $d+e$ with multiplicity $d$ at $P$. In particular, if $V$ is irreducible and $e \geq 2$ then we can take $Z$ to be points in linear general position which impose independent conditions on forms of degree $d+e$.
assumptions: Let $V$ be a reduced, equidimensional, non-degenerate subvariety of codimension two and degree $d$ in $\ensuremath{\mathbb{P}}^n$, $n \geq 3$.
Let $S$ be a hypersurface of degree $e \geq 1$ not containing any irreducible component of $V$.
Let $Y = V \cup S$.
Let $Z \subset Y$ be a finite set of points such that $[I_Z]_{d+e} = [I_Y]_{d+e}$.
conclusions: Then $Z$ admits a unique unexpected hypersurface of degree $d+e$ with multiplicity $d$ at $P$.
nodes.statement_short: Adding a hypersurface S of degree e to a codimension-2 variety gives unexpected hypersurfaces of degree d+e with a d-fold point.
nodes.label: add S

nodes.name: Proof of Corollary 2.14
nodes.statement: Let $F$ be the form defining $S$. Then \[ [I_Z]_{d+e} = [I_Y]_{d+e} = F \cdot [I_V]_d \] so \[ \dim [I_Z]_{d+e} - \binom{d+n-1}{n} = \dim [I_V]_d - \binom{d+n-1}{n} < 1 \] as we saw in the proof of Proposition \ref{Pn}. Thus $S_P \cup S$ is an unexpected hypersurface of degree $d+e$ with a singular point of multiplicity $d$ at $P$.
nodes.statement_short: [I_Z]_{d+e} = F·[I_V]_d, so the count reduces to Proposition 2.4.

nodes.name: Classification of (n,d,m) admitting unexpected hypersurfaces
nodes.statement: \ \begin{enumerate}[label={(\roman*)}] \item There exists a finite set of points $Z \subset \ensuremath{\mathbb{P}}^2$ admitting an unexpected curve of degree $d$ and multiplicity $m$ at a general point if and only if $d > m > 2$. \item For $n \geq 3$, there exists a finite set of points $Z \subset \ensuremath{\mathbb{P}}^n$ admitting an unexpected hypersurface of degree $d$ and multiplicity $m$ at a general point if and only if $d \geq m \geq 2$. \end{enumerate}
conclusions: There exists a finite set of points $Z \subset \ensuremath{\mathbb{P}}^2$ admitting an unexpected curve of degree $d$ and multiplicity $m$ at a general point if and only if $d > m > 2$.

For $n \geq 3$, there exists a finite set of points $Z \subset \ensuremath{\mathbb{P}}^n$ admitting an unexpected hypersurface of degree $d$ and multiplicity $m$ at a general point if and only if $d \geq m \geq 2$.
nodes.statement_short: Unexpected hypersurfaces of degree d with general m-fold point exist iff d>m>2 (n=2) or d>=m>=2 (n>=3).
nodes.label: m<d

nodes.name: Proof of Theorem 2.15
nodes.statement: For (i), we first note that there is an unexpected curve of degree $m+1$ and multiplicity $m$ at a general point for each $m \geq 3$. Indeed, \begin{itemize} \item $m \leq 2$. It was shown by Akesseh \cite{A} that this occurs only in characteristic 2. (See also \cite{FGST} for a different proof that shows that it does not occur in characteristic zero.) \item $m=3$. This comes from the dual of the $B_3$ arrangement \cite{DIV}. \item $m=4$. Consider the line arrangement defined by the linear factors of $$xyz(x^3-y^3)(x^3-z^3)(y^3-z^3).$$ This is a supersolvable arrangement (see definition in \S\ref{root system section}), so Theorem 3.7 of \cite{DMO} applies. In particular, the dual points give a reduced set of 12 points which admit an unexpected curve with $d=5$ and $m=4$. \item $m=5$. This follows from \cite{CHMN} Proposition 6.15, taking $k=2$. \item $m \geq 6$. This comes from the points dual to the Fermat arrangement, by \cite{CHMN} Proposition 6.15, taking $t \geq 5$. \end{itemize} \noindent It is clear that a set of points $Z$ in $\ensuremath{\mathbb{P}}^2$ cannot admit an unexpected curve whose degree and multiplicity at a general point $P$ are equal (unlike what we have seen in $\ensuremath{\mathbb{P}}^3$). Indeed, in this situation the line joining $P$ to any point of $Z$ must be a component of such an unexpected curve, so the unexpected curve is a cone with vertex $P$ over the points of $Z$. Let $d = \deg Z$ be the degree of this curve. Then $Z$ imposes independent conditions on curves of degree $d$, so $\dim [I_Z]_d = \binom{d+2}{2} - d$. Then \[ \dim [I_Z]_d - \binom{(d-1)+2}{2} = \binom{d+2}{2} - d - \binom{d+1}{2} = (d+1)-d = 1 \] so in fact the cone is not unexpected. Thus $m < d$. With this preparation, we use the same argument as was used to prove Corollary \ref{add S}. Let $Z_0$ be a set of points admitting an unexpected curve of degree $m+1$ and multiplicity $m$ at a general point $P$ and let $A$ be a plane curve of degree $d-m-1$ not passing through any point of $Z_0$. Since $P$ is general, it does not lie on $A$. Then choosing sufficiently many points on $A$ gives a unique unexpected curve of degree $d$ and multiplicity $m$ at $P$. (A similar construction also was used in \cite[Proposition 6.7]{DIV}, but see \cite[Example 7.4]{CHMN}.) Part (ii) follows from Proposition \ref{Pn} and Corollary \ref{add S}.
nodes.statement_short: Case analysis on m gives unexpected curves of degree m+1; adding a curve A extends to all d>m; d=m is impossible in P^2. Part (ii) from Proposition 2.4 and Corollary 2.14.

nodes.name: Weak and Strong Lefschetz Property
nodes.statement: Let $R/I$ be an artinian $\ensuremath{\mathbb{K}}$-algebra and let $L$ be a general linear form. Then $R/I$ satisfies the {\em Weak Lefschetz Property (WLP)} in degree $i$ if $\times L : [R/I]_i \rightarrow [R/I]_{i+1}$ has maximal rank, and we say that $R/I$ satisfies the {\em Strong Lefschetz Property (SLP)} in degree $i$ with range $k$ if $\times L^k : [R/I]_i \rightarrow [R/I]_{i+k}$ has maximal rank. We say that $R/I$ satisfies WLP (resp.\ SLP) if it does so for all $i$ (resp. for all $i$ and $k$).
nodes.statement_short: R/I has WLP in degree i if multiplication by a general linear form L has maximal rank; SLP in degree i with range k if multiplication by L^k does.

nodes.name: Unexpected hypersurfaces versus failure of SLP
nodes.statement: Let $L_1,\ldots, L_r$ be distinct linear forms on $\ensuremath{\mathbb{P}}^n$, and let $Z$ be the set of points in $\ensuremath{\mathbb{P}}^n$ dual to the hyperplanes defined by the $L_i$. Fix integers $d\geq m>1$. Then the following are equivalent: \begin{enumerate} \item[(a)] $Z$ has an unexpected hypersurface of degree $d$ with a general point $P$ of multiplicity~$m$; \item[(b)] $R/(L_1^{d},\ldots, L_r^{d})$ fails SLP in degree $i=m-1$ with range $k=d-m+1$. \end{enumerate}
nodes.origin_citation: Di Gennaro & Ilardi (DI), Theorem 13 (special case); generalizes Di Gennaro, Ilardi, Valles Theorem 5.1
assumptions: Let $L_1,\ldots, L_r$ be distinct linear forms on $\ensuremath{\mathbb{P}}^n$, and let $Z$ be the set of points in $\ensuremath{\mathbb{P}}^n$ dual to the hyperplanes defined by the $L_i$.
Fix integers $d\geq m>1$.
conclusions: $Z$ has an unexpected hypersurface of degree $d$ with a general point $P$ of multiplicity~$m$;
$R/(L_1^{d},\ldots, L_r^{d})$ fails SLP in degree $i=m-1$ with range $k=d-m+1$.
nodes.statement_short: Dual points Z have an unexpected degree-d hypersurface with general m-fold point iff R/(L_i^d) fails SLP in degree m-1 with range d-m+1.
nodes.label: SLPvUH

nodes.name: Proof of Proposition 2.17
nodes.statement: Let $L$ be a general linear form. Consider the exact sequence \begin{equation} \dots \rightarrow [R/(L_1^d, \dots, L_{r}^d)]_{m-1} \stackrel{\times L^{d-m+1}}{\longrightarrow} [R/(L_1^{d},\dots,L_{r}^{d})]_{d} \rightarrow [R/(L_1^{d},\dots,L_{r}^{d},L^{d-m+1})]_{d} \rightarrow 0. \end{equation} Let $P$ be the general point of $\ensuremath{\mathbb{P}}^n$ dual to $L$. By Macaulay duality \cite{EI} and exactness, \[ \begin{array}{rcl} \dim [I_Z \cap I_P^{m}]_{d} & = & \dim [R/(L_1^{d} , \dots, L_r^{d},L^{d-m+1})]_{d} \\ \\ & \geq & \dim [R/(L_1^d,\dots, L_r^d)]_d - \dim [R/(L_1^d,\dots,L_r^d)]_{m-1} \\ \\ & = & \displaystyle \dim [I_Z]_d - \binom{n+m-1}{n}. \end{array} \] Since (a) holds if and only if $\dim [I_Z \cap I_P^{m}]_{d}>\max(0, \dim [I_Z]_d - \binom{n+m-1}{n})$ if and only if $\dim [R/(L_1^{d} , \dots, L_r^{d},L^{d-m+1})]_{d}>\max(0, \dim [R/(L_1^d,\dots, L_r^d)]_d - \dim [R/(L_1^d,\dots,L_r^d)]_{m-1})$ if and only if (b) holds, the result follows.
nodes.statement_short: Macaulay duality applied to the exact sequence of multiplication by L^{d-m+1}, comparing dimensions.

nodes.name: Exact sequence of multiplication by a power of L
nodes.statement: \dots \rightarrow [R/(L_1^d, \dots, L_{r}^d)]_{m-1} \stackrel{\times L^{d-m+1}}{\longrightarrow} [R/(L_1^{d},\dots,L_{r}^{d})]_{d} \rightarrow [R/(L_1^{d},\dots,L_{r}^{d},L^{d-m+1})]_{d} \rightarrow 0.
nodes.label: LES

nodes.name: No unexpected curves for points in linear general position in P^2 (CHMN)
nodes.statement: For a set of points in $\ensuremath{\mathbb{P}}^2$ in linear general position (i.e., no three on a line), \cite{CHMN} shows that there is no unexpected curve of any degree, hence the corresponding ideals of powers of linear forms do not fail SLP in range 2.
assumptions: a set of points in $\ensuremath{\mathbb{P}}^2$ in linear general position (i.e., no three on a line)
conclusions: there is no unexpected curve of any degree, hence the corresponding ideals of powers of linear forms do not fail SLP in range 2

nodes.name: Failure of WLP for powers of linear forms dual to points on a space curve
nodes.statement: Let $C$ be a reduced, irreducible, non-degenerate curve of degree $d \geq 3$ in $\ensuremath{\mathbb{P}}^3$. Let $k \geq d$ be a positive integer. Let $Z$ be any set of $m \geq dk+1$ points of $C$. Let $L_1,\dots,L_m$ be the linear forms dual to the points of $Z$. In particular, $L_1,\dots,L_m$ can be chosen so that no four vanish on a point (i.e. the points of $Z$ are in linear general position). Then $R/(L_1^k,\dots,L_m^k)$ fails the WLP in degree $k-1$.
assumptions: Let $C$ be a reduced, irreducible, non-degenerate curve of degree $d \geq 3$ in $\ensuremath{\mathbb{P}}^3$.
Let $k \geq d$ be a positive integer.
Let $Z$ be any set of $m \geq dk+1$ points of $C$.
Let $L_1,\dots,L_m$ be the linear forms dual to the points of $Z$.
conclusions: Then $R/(L_1^k,\dots,L_m^k)$ fails the WLP in degree $k-1$.
nodes.statement_short: Powers L_i^k of forms dual to many points on a space curve of degree d<=k fail WLP in degree k-1.
nodes.label: WLP for curves in P3

nodes.name: Proof of Corollary 2.18
nodes.statement: The statement about linear general position is immediate since $C$ is reduced, irreducible and non-degenerate. From Corollary \ref{higher deg} we know that $C$ has an unexpected surface of degree $k$ with a general point $P$ of multiplicity $k$, so we have $\dim [I_C \cap I_P^k]_k>\max(0,\dim [I_C]_k - \binom{k+2}{3})$. But by B\'ezout's theorem we have $[I_Z]_k = [I_C]_k$ so we obtain $\dim [I_Z \cap I_P^k]_k>\max(0,\dim [I_Z]_k - \binom{k+2}{3})$, hence $Z$ has an unexpected surface of degree $k$ with multiplicity $k$ at $P$, so $R/(L_1^k,\dots,L_m^k)$ fails the WLP in degree $k-1$ by Proposition \ref{SLPvUH}.
nodes.statement_short: Corollary 2.12 plus Bezout gives an unexpected surface for Z; Proposition 2.17 converts it to failure of WLP.

nodes.name: 31 points on a twisted cubic fail WLP
nodes.statement: Let $Z$ consist of a set of 31 points on a twisted cubic $C$. Let $L_1,\dots,L_{31}$ be the linear forms dual to these points. Then for each $3 \leq k \leq 10$, the algebra \[ R/(L_1^k,\dots,L_{31}^k) \] fails the WLP from degree $k-1$ to degree $k$. We remark that this does not mean that these are the only powers that fail WLP or that the given degrees are the only places where it fails. Experimentally with CoCoA \cite{cocoa} we have considered the case of 31 points on the twisted cubic as above, but allowed different $k$. When $k=2$ the algebra has WLP. When $3 \leq k \leq 10$ it fails from degree $k-1$ to degree $k$ as claimed, but also in certain other degrees (depending on $k$). For $k \geq 11$ it still fails in several degrees, but now it does {\em not} fail from degree $k-1$ to $k$.
nodes.statement_short: 31 points on a twisted cubic: R/(L_i^k) fails WLP from degree k-1 to k for 3<=k<=10, with CoCoA experiments for other k.

nodes.name: Failure of WLP for linear forms in at least five variables
nodes.statement: Let $n \geq 4$ and $k \geq 3$. Set \[ f(n, k) = \begin{cases} \binom{n+k}{n} - \binom{n+k-2}{n} - \binom{n + \frac{k}{2}}{n} + \binom{n -2 + \frac{k}{2}}{n} & \text{ if $k$ is even} \\ \binom{n+k}{n} - \binom{n+k-2}{n} - 2 \binom{n + \frac{k-1}{2}}{n} + 2 \binom{n + \frac{k-3}{2}}{n-1} & \text{ if $k$ is odd.} \end{cases} \] Choose any integer $N \geq f(n,k)$. Then there exist linear forms $L_1,\dots,L_N \in \ensuremath{\mathbb{K}}[x_0,\dots,x_n] = R$ satisfying \begin{itemize} \item no $n+1$ of the linear forms have a common zero, and \item $R/(L_1^k,\dots,L_N^k)$ fails the WLP from degree $k-1$ to degree $k$. \end{itemize}
assumptions: Let $n \geq 4$ and $k \geq 3$.
Choose any integer $N \geq f(n,k)$.
conclusions: $R/(L_1^k,\dots,L_N^k)$ fails the WLP from degree $k-1$ to degree $k$.
nodes.statement_short: For n>=4, k>=3 and N>=f(n,k) there are N linear forms in general position whose k-th powers fail WLP from degree k-1 to k.
nodes.label: WLP Pn cons

nodes.name: Proof of Corollary 2.20
nodes.statement: We recall that we can always find an irreducible, non-degenerate subvariety $V$ of codimension 2 and degree $k$ in $\ensuremath{\mathbb{P}}^n$. In fact, if $k$ is even we take $V$ as an intersection of a general form of degree $\frac{k}{2}$ and a general quadric. If $k$ is odd we take $V$ as a general arithmetically Cohen-Macaulay subscheme with a minimal free resolution of the form \[ 0 \rightarrow R(- {\textstyle \frac{k+3}{2} })^2 \rightarrow R(- {\textstyle \frac{k+1}{2} })^2 \oplus R(-2) \rightarrow R \rightarrow R/I_V \rightarrow 0 \] (obtained, for example, by linking from a linear space of codimension 2 using the complete intersection of a quadric and a form of degree $\frac{k+1}{2}$). Using this sequence, or the Koszul resolution if $k$ is even, we obtain \[ \dim [R/I_V]_k = f (n, k). \] Since $V$ is irreducible, it makes sense to speak of a general set of points on $V$. Let $Z$ be a general set of $N$ points on $V$. From the generality of $Z$ we have \[ \dim [R/I_Z]_k = \min \{ \dim [R/I_V]_k , |Z| \}, \] hence $\dim [I_V]_k = \dim [I_Z]_k$. By Proposition 2.4 we then have that the cone over $V$ with vertex at a general point $P$ is an unexpected hypersurface of degree $k$ and multiplicity $k$ at $P$. Then the argument in the proof of Corollary 2.16 can be extended to our situation to show that the multiplication from degree $k-1$ to degree $k$ by a general linear form has an unexpectedly large cokernel, i.e. maximal rank does not hold. Since $Z$ is general on $V$ and $V$ is irreducible and non-degenerate, $Z$ is a set of points in linear general position, and this implies the condition on the linear forms not to have a common zero.
nodes.statement_short: Construct an irreducible codimension-2 variety V of degree k (complete intersection or linked ACM), take general points on it, and apply Proposition 2.4.

nodes.name: Characterization of SLP failure for powers of linear forms
nodes.statement: Let $R = \ensuremath{\mathbb{K}}[x_0,\dots,x_n]$. Fix positive integers $d\geq m$. Then there exists an ideal $I = (L_1^d,\dots, L_e^d)$ (for suitable $e$) for which \[ \times L^{d-m+1} : [R/I]_{m-1} \rightarrow [R/I]_d \] fails to have maximal rank if and only if one of the following holds. \begin{itemize} \item[(i)] We have $n = 2$ and $d > m > 2$. \item[(ii)] We have $n \geq 3$ and $d \geq m \geq 2$. \end{itemize} In both cases this means that $R/I$ fails the SLP in degree $m-1$ and range $d-m+1$.
assumptions: Let $R = \ensuremath{\mathbb{K}}[x_0,\dots,x_n]$.
Fix positive integers $d\geq m$.
conclusions: We have $n = 2$ and $d > m > 2$.
We have $n \geq 3$ and $d \geq m \geq 2$.
nodes.statement_short: Some ideal of d-th powers of linear forms fails maximal rank for ×L^{d-m+1} in degree m-1 iff d>m>2 (n=2) or d>=m>=2 (n>=3).
nodes.label: fail SLP

nodes.name: Proof of Corollary 2.21
nodes.statement: This follows immediately from Theorem \ref{m<d} by applying Proposition \ref{SLPvUH}.
nodes.statement_short: Combine Theorem 2.15 with Proposition 2.17.

nodes.name: Surjectivity versus injectivity and the Schenck-Seceleanu theorem
nodes.statement: \begin{enumerate} \item Note that Corollary \ref{fail SLP} (and similarly for the earlier results) is not necessarily about failure of surjectivity. The proof only shows that the cokernel of $\times L^{d-m+1}$ is bigger than expected, which means failure of surjectivity if $\dim [R/I]_{m-1} \geq \dim [R/I]_d$, and it means failure of injectivity if $\dim [R/I]_{m-1} \leq \dim [R/I]_d$. \item In \cite{SS}, Schenck and Seceleanu proved the striking result that for {\em every} ideal of the form $I = (L_1^{a_1},\dots,L_e^{a_e})$ in the ring $\ensuremath{\mathbb{K}}[x,y,z]$, the quotient $R/I$ has the WLP. In the case that all $a_i$ are equal to some $d$, we can recover this result from Corollary \ref{fail SLP}. Indeed, this is the case $n=2$. Checking whether WLP holds amounts to considering the case $m=d$ (since we are studying $\times L^1$), and Corollary \ref{fail SLP} says that in this case maximal rank always holds. \end{enumerate}
nodes.statement_short: The failure may be of injectivity or surjectivity; Corollary 2.21 with n=2, m=d recovers Schenck-Seceleanu's WLP theorem for equal powers.

nodes.name: Schenck-Seceleanu theorem
nodes.statement: In \cite{SS}, Schenck and Seceleanu proved the striking result that for {\em every} ideal of the form $I = (L_1^{a_1},\dots,L_e^{a_e})$ in the ring $\ensuremath{\mathbb{K}}[x,y,z]$, the quotient $R/I$ has the WLP.
assumptions: for {\em every} ideal of the form $I = (L_1^{a_1},\dots,L_e^{a_e})$ in the ring $\ensuremath{\mathbb{K}}[x,y,z]$
conclusions: the quotient $R/I$ has the WLP

nodes.name: Simplicial real arrangement
nodes.statement: It is a simplicial real arrangement. (This means that the lines divide the real projective plane into triangles.)

nodes.name: Melchior's inequality
nodes.statement: (If $t_k$ denotes the number of points where exactly $k$ lines meet, an inequality of Melchior \cite{Me} for real arrangements of $d>2$ lines with $t_d=0$ states that $t_2\geq 3+\sum_{k>2}(k-3)t_k$.
assumptions: for real arrangements of $d>2$ lines with $t_d=0$

nodes.name: Free line arrangement
nodes.statement: It is free (meaning that if $F$ is the product of the linear forms defining the lines dual to the points of $Z$, then there are no second syzygies for the Jacobian ideal $J_F=(F_x,F_y,F_z)$; i.e., the syzygy bundle for $J_F$ is free.)

nodes.name: Supersolvable line arrangement
nodes.statement: A line arrangement in the projective plane is {\em supersolvable} if there is a so-called {\em modular} point, i.e., a point $P$ where two or more of the lines meet such that if $Q$ is any other point where two or more of the lines meet, then the line through $P$ and $Q$ is a line in the arrangement.
nodes.genus: line arrangement in the projective plane
differentia: there is a so-called {\em modular} point

nodes.name: Multiplicity of a point for a line arrangement
nodes.statement: The {\em multiplicity} of a point with respect to a line arrangement is just the number of lines in the arrangement containing the point.
nodes.definiendum: multiplicity of a point with respect to a line arrangement

nodes.name: Maximum multiplicity points of supersolvable arrangements are modular
nodes.statement: When a line arrangement is supersolvable, every point of maximum multiplicity is modular (but not every modular point need have maximum multiplicity) \cite{AT} (only the arXiv version includes the proof).
assumptions: When a line arrangement is supersolvable
conclusions: every point of maximum multiplicity is modular

nodes.name: Di Marca-Malara-Oneto theorem on supersolvable arrangements
nodes.statement: The result of \cite{DMO} says the point scheme $Z_A$ dual to the lines of a supersolvable line arrangement $A$ has an unexpected curve of degree $m_A$ with respect to $X=(m_A-1)P$ for a general point $P$ if and only if $2m_A<d_A$, where $d_A$ is the number of lines in the arrangement and $m_A$ is the maximum multiplicity of a point for $A$, and in this case the unexpected curve is unique.
assumptions: a supersolvable line arrangement $A$
conclusions: has an unexpected curve of degree $m_A$ with respect to $X=(m_A-1)P$ for a general point $P$ if and only if $2m_A<d_A$
nodes.statement_short: The dual points of a supersolvable arrangement have an unexpected curve of degree m_A (max multiplicity) iff 2m_A < d_A; then it is unique.

nodes.name: B3 points have a unique unexpected quartic
nodes.statement: Since $m_{B_3}=4$ and $d_{B_3}=9$, it follows that $Z_{B_3}$ has a unique unexpected curve of degree 4.
conclusions: $Z_{B_3}$ has a unique unexpected curve of degree 4

nodes.name: Roots of B3
nodes.statement: The roots of $B_3$ can be defined as the integer vector solutions $(a,b,c)\in\ensuremath{\mathbb{R}}^3$ to $1\leq a^2+b^2+c^2\leq2$.

nodes.name: Point set Z_A of a root system
nodes.statement: The set-up then is: a root system $A$ gives a finite set of vectors of $\ensuremath{\mathbb{R}}^n$ for some $n$. Each root gives a point in $\ensuremath{\mathbb{P}}^{n-1}$ and the set of these points for the given root system $A$ gives the point set we denote by $Z_A$. The codimension 1 linear subspaces normal to the roots define the hyperplanes of the arrangement corresponding to $A$ which we also refer to by $A$.
nodes.statement_short: Each root of a root system A in R^n gives a point of P^{n-1}; Z_A is the set of these points, and A also names the dual hyperplane arrangement.

nodes.name: Generic point and the ring S
nodes.statement: In principle, given a finite set of points $Z\subset\ensuremath{\mathbb{P}}^n$ and a general point $P=[a_0:\cdots:a_n]$, to find an unexpected hypersurface for $Z+mP$ computationally one takes $P$ to be the generic point $P=[1:\frac{a_1}{a_0}:\cdots:\frac{a_n}{a_0}]$ and works as usual in the homogeneous coordinate ring $S=\ensuremath{\mathbb{K}}(\frac{a_1}{a_0},\ldots,\frac{a_n}{a_0})[x_0,\ldots,x_n]= \ensuremath{\mathbb{K}}[\ensuremath{\mathbb{P}}^n_{\ensuremath{\mathbb{K}}(\frac{a_1}{a_0},\ldots,\frac{a_n}{a_0})}]$.
nodes.statement_short: Treat the general point P as the generic point over K(a_1/a_0,...,a_n/a_0) and work in S, the coordinate ring over that field.

nodes.name: Bi-graded ring R
nodes.statement: However, it can be convenient and more efficient to work in the bi-graded ring $R=\ensuremath{\mathbb{K}}[a_0,\ldots,a_n][x_0,\ldots,x_n]$.

nodes.name: The bi-homogeneous form F^*
nodes.statement: Thus given a form $F\in S$ of degree $d$ but which is not in $\ensuremath{\mathbb{K}}$, there is (up to scalars in $\ensuremath{\mathbb{K}}$) a unique factorization $F=BG/H$, where $B$ and $H$ are relatively prime forms in $\ensuremath{\mathbb{K}}[a_0,\ldots,a_n]$ and $G\in R$ is bi-homogeneous with no factors of bi-degree $(a,0)$ with $a>0$; its bi-degree is $(t,d)$, where $t=\deg(H)-\deg(B)$. We denote $G$ by $F^*$.
nodes.statement_short: Clearing denominators, F = BG/H with G bi-homogeneous in R without pure-a factors; G is denoted F^*.

nodes.name: The dehomogenized form G°
nodes.statement: Given any bi-homogeneous element $G\in R$ of bi-degree $(t,d)$, we denote $G/a_0^t$ by $G^\circ$.

nodes.name: Passing between S and the bi-graded ring R
nodes.statement: Let $S$ and $R$ be as above. Let $P$ be the point $[1:\frac{a_1}{a_0}:\cdots:\frac{a_n}{a_0}] \in\ensuremath{\mathbb{P}}^n_{\ensuremath{\mathbb{K}}(\frac{a_1}{a_0},\ldots,\frac{a_n}{a_0})}$. For any $m \geq 1$, let $I_{mP}$ denote the ideal $(I_P)^m$ in $S$, and let $J_{mP}$ denote the ideal $(J_P)^m$ in $R$, where $J_P=(\{a_ix_j-a_jx_i: i\neq j\})$ (hence $(J_P)^m$ is generated by elements of bi-degree $(m,m)$). Now let $d>0$ and $t \geq 0$, let $F\in S$ be a nonzero form of degree $d$, and let $G\in R$ be a nonzero, nonconstant bi-homogeneous form of bi-degree $(t,d)$. \begin{enumerate} \item[(a)] As ideals in $S$ we have $(F)=((F^*)^\circ)$. \item[(b)] If $F$ is irreducible, then so are $F^*$ and $(F^*)^\circ$. \item[(c)] If $G$ is irreducible, then so are $G^\circ$ and $(G^\circ)^*$, and as ideals in $R$ we have $(G)=((G^\circ)^*)$. \item[(d)] If $F\in I_{mP}$, then $d\geq m$ and $F^*\in J_{mP}$ so we see that $F^*$ has bi-degree $(s,d)$ for some $s$ with $s\geq m$. \item[(e)] If $G\in J_{mP}$, then $G^\circ\in I_{mP}$. \end{enumerate}
assumptions: Let $S$ and $R$ be as above.
let $F\in S$ be a nonzero form of degree $d$,
let $G\in R$ be a nonzero, nonconstant bi-homogeneous form of bi-degree $(t,d)$.
conclusions: As ideals in $S$ we have $(F)=((F^*)^\circ)$.
If $F$ is irreducible, then so are $F^*$ and $(F^*)^\circ$.
If $F\in I_{mP}$, then $d\geq m$ and $F^*\in J_{mP}$
nodes.statement_short: The operations F→F^* and G→G° preserve principal ideals, irreducibility and membership in powers of the ideal of the generic point.
nodes.label: StEx

nodes.name: Proof of Lemma 3.1
nodes.statement: (a) Since $F=BF^*/H=B(F^*)^\circ a_0^t/H$, where $t=\deg(H)-\deg(B)$, we see that $F$ and $(F^*)^\circ$ differ by $Ba_0^t/H$, which is a unit in $S$. (b) Note that $F$ and $(F^*)^\circ$ differ by a unit factor in $S$, so one is irreducible if and only if the other is. Also, $F^*$ by construction has no factors of bi-degree $(f,0)$ with $f>0$, so if $F^*$ fails to be irreducible, it factors as $F^*=AB$ where $A$ and $B$ have bi-degree $(a,d_A)$ and $(b,d_B)$ with $d_A,d_B>0$ and $d_A+d_B=d$. But then $(F^*)^\circ=A^\circ B^\circ$ is a product of factors of positive degree and hence not irreducible. (c) If $G^\circ$ is not irreducible, then $G^\circ=AB$ where both $A$ and $B$ have positive degree $d_A$ and $d_B$, so we have $G=\alpha A^*\beta B^*$ where $A^*$ and $B^*$ have bi-degrees $(a,d_A)$ and $(b,d_B)$, and $\alpha$ and $\beta$ have bi-degrees $(t_\alpha,0)$ and $(t_\beta,0)$. Since $R$ is a UFD, the denominators in the right hand side of the expression $G=\alpha A^*\beta B^*$ must cancel with factors of the numerators of the expression $\alpha A^*\beta B^*$ and this does not affect the values of $d_A$ or $d_B$, so we may assume that $\alpha,\beta, A^*, B^*$ all are in $R$ and $A^*$ and $B^*$ have bi-degrees $(a',d_A)$ and $(b',d_B)$, where the simplification might have changed $a$ and $b$ but will have left $d_a$ and $d_B$ unchanged. Since $d_A$ and $d_B$ are both positive, $G$ has nonunit factors so $G$ is not irreducible. Now note that irreducibility of $G^\circ$ implies that for $(G^\circ)^*$ by (b). Finally, by construction, if $G$ is irreducible with bi-degree $(t,d)$ where $d>0$, then $G=c(G^\circ)^*$ for some nonzero $c\in\ensuremath{\mathbb{K}}$, hence $(G)=((G^\circ)^*)$. (d) Since $F\in I_{mP}$, by (a) we have $\frac{F^*}{a_0^s}=(F^*)^\circ\in I_{mP}$, where $(s,d)$ is the bi-degree of $F^*$, and since $d$ is the degree of $(F^*)^\circ$ and since $(F^*)^\circ\in I_{mP}$ we have $d\geq m$. Now let $$D\big(\frac{a_1}{a_0},\ldots,\frac{a_n}{a_0},\frac{x_1}{x_0},\ldots,\frac{x_n}{x_0}\big)= F^*\big(\frac{a_0}{a_0},\ldots,\frac{a_n}{a_0},\frac{x_0}{x_0},\frac{x_1}{x_0},\ldots,\frac{x_n}{x_0}\big)=\frac{F^*(a_0,\ldots,a_n,x_0,\ldots,x_n)}{a_0^sx_0^d},$$ so as a rational function $D$ has bi-degree $(0,0)$, but as a polynomial in $\ensuremath{\mathbb{K}}(\frac{a_1}{a_0},\ldots,\frac{a_n}{a_0})[\frac{x_1}{x_0},\ldots,\frac{x_n}{x_0}]$, $D$ has degree $\delta\leq d$. Moreover, since $x_0\not\in I_P$, we have $D\in I_{mQ}$ where $Q$ is the point $Q=(\frac{a_1}{a_0},\ldots,\frac{a_n}{a_0})$ in the affine open subset $\ensuremath{\mathbb{K}}(\frac{a_1}{a_0},\ldots,\frac{a_n}{a_0})^n$ away from $x_0=0$. Now translate $Q$ to the origin; i.e., consider $$H\big(\frac{a_1}{a_0},\ldots,\frac{a_n}{a_0},\frac{x_1}{x_0},\ldots,\frac{x_n}{x_0}\big)= D\big(\frac{a_1}{a_0},\ldots,\frac{a_n}{a_0},\frac{x_1}{x_0}+\frac{a_1}{a_0},\ldots,\frac{x_n}{x_0}+\frac{a_n}{a_0}\big).$$ Note that $$a_0^{s+d}x_0^dH=a_0^{s+d}x_0^dF^*\big(\frac{a_0}{a_0},\ldots,\frac{a_n}{a_0},\frac{x_0}{x_0},\frac{x_1}{x_0}+\frac{a_1}{a_0},\ldots,\frac{x_n}{x_0}+\frac{a_n}{a_0}\big)=$$ $$F^*\big(a_0,\ldots,a_n,a_0x_0,a_0x_1+a_1x_0,\ldots,a_0x_n+a_nx_0\big)\in R$$ is a bi-homogeneous polynomial of bi-degree $(s+d,d)$. Since $H$ has multiplicity $m$ at the origin (with respect to the variables $\frac{x_1}{x_0},\ldots,\frac{x_n}{x_0}$), $H$ is a sum of terms where each term consists of a monomial in $\frac{x_1}{x_0},\ldots,\frac{x_n}{x_0}$ of degree at least $m$ and at most $d$, times a polynomial in the variables $\frac{a_1}{a_0},\ldots,\frac{a_n}{a_0}$ of degree at most $s+d$. Thus each term is of the form $$c\big(\frac{a_1}{a_0},\ldots,\frac{a_n}{a_0}\big)\big(\frac{x_1}{x_0}\big)^{i_1}\cdots\big(\frac{x_n}{x_0}\big)^{i_n}$$ where $m\leq \sum_ji_j\leq d$ and $c$ has degree at most $s+d$. Thus multiplying by $a_0^{s+d}x_0^d$ clears the denominators. Translating back we recover $D$; i.e., $$D\big(\frac{a_1}{a_0},\ldots,\frac{a_n}{a_0},\frac{x_1}{x_0},\ldots,\frac{x_n}{x_0}\big)= H\big(\frac{a_1}{a_0},\ldots,\frac{a_n}{a_0},\frac{x_1}{x_0}-\frac{a_1}{a_0},\ldots,\frac{x_n}{x_0}-\frac{a_n}{a_0}\big),$$ but each term becomes $$c\big(\frac{a_1}{a_0},\ldots,\frac{a_n}{a_0}\big)\big(\frac{x_1}{x_0}-\frac{a_1}{a_0}\big)^{i_1}\cdots\big(\frac{x_n}{x_0}-\frac{a_n}{a_0}\big)^{i_n} =c\big(\frac{a_1}{a_0},\ldots,\frac{a_n}{a_0}\big)\big(\frac{a_0x_1-a_1x_0}{a_0x_0}\big)^{i_1}\cdots\big(\frac{a_0x_n-a_nx_0}{a_0x_0}\big)^{i_n}$$ and multiplying by $a_0^{2d+s}x_0^d$ we obtain $$C(a_0,\ldots,a_n)(a_0x_1-a_1x_0)^{i_1}\cdots(a_0x_n-a_nx_0)^{i_n}$$ where $C$ is homogeneous in the variables $a_i$ of degree $s+d$, and $$(a_0x_1-a_1x_0)^{i_1}\cdots(a_0x_n-a_nx_0)^{i_n}\in J_{mP}.$$ Thus $a_0^{2d+s}x_0^dH\big(\frac{a_1}{a_0},\ldots,\frac{a_n}{a_0},\frac{x_1}{x_0}-\frac{a_1}{a_0},\ldots,\frac{x_n}{x_0}-\frac{a_n}{a_0}\big)= a_0^{2d+s}x_0^dD=a_0^{2d}F^*\in J_{mP}$. But by \cite[Corollary 7.10]{BV}, since $J_P$ is the ideal generated by the maximal minors of a $2 \times (n+1)$ matrix of indeterminates, namely the two sets of variables, the powers $J_{mP}$ are primary for $J_P$. Since no power of $a_0$ is in $J_{mP}$, we see that $F^*\in J_{mP}$. (e) If $G\in J_{mP}$, then $G=\sum_s H_sM_s$ where each $M_s$ is a product of $m$ forms such as $a_ix_j-a_jx_i$ and each $H_s$ is a bi-homogeneous form of bi-degree $(t-m,d-m)$. So $G^\circ$ is obtained by dividing $G$ by $a_0^t$, hence we get $G^\circ=\sum_s H_s^\circ M_s^\circ$, and each $M_s^\circ$ is a product of $m$ forms such as $(a_ix_j-a_jx_i)/a_0$, each of which is in $I_P$. Thus $G^\circ\in I_{mP}$.
nodes.statement_short: Item by item; (d) translates the generic point to the origin, clears denominators and uses that powers of the 2x2-minor ideal J_P are primary (Bruns-Vetter).

nodes.name: B_{n+1} root systems give unexpected hypersurfaces
nodes.statement: It seems likely that the root system $B_{n+1}$, which gives a point set $Z_{B_{n+1}}$ in $\ensuremath{\mathbb{P}}^n$, gives rise to an unexpected hypersurface for each $n\geq 2$, but our verifications of unexpectedness are computational and so are limited to a few smaller values of $n$.
nodes.statement_short: Z_{B_{n+1}} in P^n should admit an unexpected hypersurface for every n>=2; verified only computationally for small n.

nodes.name: Universal script
nodes.statement: Given a finite set of points $Z\subset\ensuremath{\mathbb{P}}^n$ we use the following script to check whether $Z$ has an unexpected hypersurface of degree $d$ vanishing on $mP$ for a general point $P=[a_0:\cdots:a_n]$. Assuming that the computation of rank given by Macaulay2 is reliable, running the script on an example gives a rigorous proof of whether the example is unexpected or not. The idea of the script is to construct the matrix $N$ expressing the conditions imposed on all forms $F$ of degree $d$ by the points of $Z$, together with the conditions imposed for $F$ to vanish to order $m$ at a point $P=[a_0:\ldots:a_n]$ with indeterminate coordinates $a_i$ represented in the scripts with new variables. Thus if we enumerate the monomials of degree $d$ in $n+1$ variables $x_i$ as $b_1,\ldots,b_{\binom{n+d}{n}}$, then $N$ will be a matrix with $|Z|+\binom{n+m-1}{n}$ rows and $\binom{n+d}{n}$ columns. A form $F=\sum_ic_ib_i$ vanishes on $Z$ and on $mP$ if and only if $Nc=0$, where $c$ is the coefficient vector $c=(c_1,\ldots,c_{\binom{n+d}{n}})^T$. We can regard $N$ as consisting of two matrices, $Q_1$ and $Q_2$, where $Q_1$ comprises the top $|Z|$ rows of $N$ and gives the conditions imposed by the points of $Z$, and $Q_2$ comprises the bottom $\binom{n+m-1}{n}$ rows of $N$ giving the conditions imposed by the fat point $mP$. Thus the entries of $Q_1$ are scalars in the ground field, but the entries of $Q_2$ are the order $m-1$ partials of the monomials $b_i$ evaluated at $P$. Then $Z$ has unexpected hypersurfaces of degree $d$ with a general point $P$ of multiplicity $m$ exactly when $$\dim \ker N > \max(0,\binom{n+d}{n}-\ensuremath{\mathrm{rank}}\hspace{1pt}(Q_1)-\ensuremath{\mathrm{rank}}\hspace{1pt}(Q_2)),$$ and in this case the coefficient vectors $c$ of the unexpected hypersurfaces are precisely the nontrivial elements of $\ker N$. The script which does this is given below. The section marked CODE BLOCK is where one puts in the list of the points of $Z$ (or where one puts in code needed to generate the list; see the examples). For now we exhibit code which works when the points of $Z$ are defined over the rationals. Subtleties arise when coordinates in an extension field are needed. We discuss that later. Apart from output indicating current status of the computation, the script output indicates exactly when it finds an unexpected hypersurface. An output of the form $(n,d,m,edim,adim)$ means that there is a hypersurface for $Z$ in $\ensuremath{\mathbb{P}}^n$ of degree $d$ with a generic point of multiplicity $m$ (that is a point whose coordinates are variables); the vector space of unexpected forms has expected dimension edim and actual dimension adim (where edim can be negative if the number of conditions imposed by $mp$ is greater than the dimension of $[I_Z]_d$). If for a given $n,d,m$ there is no output, then $Z$ has no unexpected hypersurface in $\ensuremath{\mathbb{P}}^n$ of degree $d$ with a general point $P$ of multiplicity $m$. We will refer to the script below as the {\it universal script}. \begin{verbatim} for n from 2 to 6 do { -- Loop over dim 2 to 6 R=QQ[x_0..x_n]; -- Define coordinate ring S=frac(QQ[a_0..a_n]); --Define ring for generic point CODE BLOCK for Pts={...}; -- Insert the list of the points of Z here print {"n=",n,"#Pts=",#Pts}; -- Print completion status indicator for d from 2 to 6 do { -- Loop over degree Md=flatten entries(basis(d,R)); -- Create deg d monomial basis for m from 2 to d do { -- Loop over multiplicity m print {"d=",d,"m=",m}; -- Print completion status indicator Mm=flatten entries(basis(m-1,R)); -- Create deg m-1 monomial basis A={}; -- A will contain the list of rows for transpose of matrix Q1 apply(Md,i->(N={};for s from 0 to #Pts-1 do N=N|{sub(i,matrix{Pts_s})};A=A|{N})); D={}; -- D will contain the list of rows for transpose of matrix Q2 apply(Md,i->(N={};for s from 0 to #Mm-1 do N=N|{diff(Mm_s,i)};D=D|{N})); Q1=transpose matrix A; -- Q1 is defined over R Q2=transpose matrix D; -- Q2 is defined over R M={}; for i from 0 to n do M=M|{a_i}; -- M is the coord vector for generic point Q1S=sub(Q1,S); -- Q1 is now defined to be over S Q2S=sub(Q2,matrix{M}); -- Swap x variables for a variables N=Q1S||Q2S; expdim=#Md - (rank Q1S) - (rank Q2S); actdim=#Md-(rank N); if actdim > expdim and actdim > 0 then print {"n=",n,"d=",d,"m=",m,"edim=",expdim,"adim=",actdim}}}} \end{verbatim}
output: An output of the form $(n,d,m,edim,adim)$ means that there is a hypersurface for $Z$ in $\ensuremath{\mathbb{P}}^n$ of degree $d$ with a generic point of multiplicity $m$
nodes.statement_short: Macaulay2 script testing unexpectedness: stack point-evaluation rows Q1 and generic-point partial-derivative rows Q2 into N and compare dim ker N with the expected dimension. Loops over n, d and m<=d.

nodes.name: Define rings
nodes.statement: R=QQ[x_0..x_n]; -- Define coordinate ring S=frac(QQ[a_0..a_n]); --Define ring for generic point
nodes.statement_short: Coordinate ring and fraction field for the generic point.

nodes.name: Insert points of Z
nodes.statement: CODE BLOCK for Pts={...}; -- Insert the list of the points of Z here
nodes.statement_short: Supply the coordinates of the points of Z.

nodes.name: Loop over degree d
nodes.statement: for d from 2 to 6 do { -- Loop over degree Md=flatten entries(basis(d,R)); -- Create deg d monomial basis for m from 2 to d do { -- Loop over multiplicity m print {"d=",d,"m=",m}; -- Print completion status indicator Mm=flatten entries(basis(m-1,R)); -- Create deg m-1 monomial basis A={}; -- A will contain the list of rows for transpose of matrix Q1 apply(Md,i->(N={};for s from 0 to #Pts-1 do N=N|{sub(i,matrix{Pts_s})};A=A|{N})); D={}; -- D will contain the list of rows for transpose of matrix Q2 apply(Md,i->(N={};for s from 0 to #Mm-1 do N=N|{diff(Mm_s,i)};D=D|{N})); Q1=transpose matrix A; -- Q1 is defined over R Q2=transpose matrix D; -- Q2 is defined over R M={}; for i from 0 to n do M=M|{a_i}; -- M is the coord vector for generic point Q1S=sub(Q1,S); -- Q1 is now defined to be over S Q2S=sub(Q2,matrix{M}); -- Swap x variables for a variables N=Q1S||Q2S; expdim=#Md - (rank Q1S) - (rank Q2S); actdim=#Md-(rank N); if actdim > expdim and actdim > 0 then print {"n=",n,"d=",d,"m=",m,"edim=",expdim,"adim=",actdim}}}}
nodes.statement_short: For each degree d from 2 to 6.

nodes.name: Degree-d monomials
nodes.statement: Md=flatten entries(basis(d,R)); -- Create deg d monomial basis
nodes.statement_short: List the monomials of degree d.

nodes.name: Loop over multiplicity m

nodes.name: Bi-degree of F^* for unexpected varieties
nodes.statement: In fact, given a form $$F\in S=\ensuremath{\mathbb{K}}\big(\frac{a_1}{a_0},\ldots,\frac{a_n}{a_0}\big)[x_0,\ldots,x_n]$$ defining an unexpected variety of degree $d$ with a general point $P$ of multiplicity $m$, one has by Lemma \ref{StEx}(d) that the bi-homogeneous form $F^*(a,x)\in R=\ensuremath{\mathbb{K}}[a_0,\ldots,a_n][x_0,\ldots,x_n]$ has bi-degree $(t,d)$ for some $t\geq m$.
conclusions: the bi-homogeneous form $F^*(a,x)\in R=\ensuremath{\mathbb{K}}[a_0,\ldots,a_n][x_0,\ldots,x_n]$ has bi-degree $(t,d)$ for some $t\geq m$

nodes.name: Tangent cone
nodes.statement: Let $W\subset \ensuremath{\mathbb{A}}^n$ be a hypersurface in affine space defined by a reduced polynomial $F$. We first recall what the tangent cone is for $W$ at a point $P\in W$. Write $F$ as a sum $F=F_0+F_1+\cdots$ of polynomials $F_i \in I(P)^i$ where each $F_i$ is homogeneous of degree $i$ in coordinates centered at the point $P$. Let $j$ be the least index such that $F_j\neq0$. Then $F_j=0$ defines the tangent cone to $W$ at $P$.
nodes.statement_short: The tangent cone of W at P is defined by the lowest-degree nonzero homogeneous part of F in coordinates centred at P.

nodes.name: Differentiation action F·G
nodes.statement: Given two polynomials $F$ and $G$, let $F\cdot G$ denote the action of differentiation, so $$(2x_0^2x_1+x_3)\cdot (x_0^3x_1^2x_3)=(2x_0^2x_1)\cdot (x_0^3x_1^2x_3)+x_3\cdot (x_0^3x_1^2x_3)=24x_0x_1x_3+x_0^3x_1^2.$$

nodes.name: Monomial enumeration mu_j
nodes.statement: To compute the tangent cone of $W$ at a point $P$ of multiplicity $m$, let $\mu_j$ be an enumeration of the monomials of degree $m$.

nodes.name: Factorial normalizers c_j
nodes.statement: Let $c_j=\mu_j\cdot\mu_j$ be the factorial expression obtained by differentiating $\mu_j$ against itself (this is needed for the Taylor expansion).

nodes.name: Tangent cone form H_P
nodes.statement: Then the tangent cone of $W$ at $P$ is defined by the degree $m$ form \begin{equation} H_P=\sum_j \frac{((\mu_j\cdot H)(P))\mu_j}{c_j}. \end{equation}
nodes.statement_short: The projective tangent cone at an m-fold point P is the degree-m Taylor term H_P = sum_j ((mu_j·H)(P)) mu_j / c_j.

nodes.name: Tangent cone form formula
nodes.statement: H_P=\sum_j \frac{((\mu_j\cdot H)(P))\mu_j}{c_j}.

nodes.name: Tangent cones for the cone construction
nodes.statement: As an example we consider the tangent cones for the cone construction of \S\ref{cone section}. Assume $Z$ is a finite set of points in $\ensuremath{\mathbb{P}}^n_\ensuremath{\mathbb{K}}$ and that the space $V\subset [S]_d$ of forms vanishing on the points has the property that there is (up to multiplication by a scalar) a unique form $F\in V$ with a point of multiplicity $d$ at a general point $P=[a_0:\ldots:a_n]\in\ensuremath{\mathbb{P}}^n$. Applying an idea similar to that of Remark \ref{need fewer pts}, remove points if necessary so that we are left with a subset $\{P_1,\ldots,P_r\}$ of $Z$ of $r=\binom{d+n}{n} - \binom{d-1+n}{n} -1$ points. (Now $F$ is not unexpected.) Then $F^*\in R=\ensuremath{\mathbb{K}}[a_0,\ldots,a_n][x_0,\ldots,x_n]$ and by Lemma \ref{StEx}(d) $F^*$ is bi-homogeneous of bi-degree $(\delta,d)$ with $\delta\geq d$. Let $M_j$ be an enumeration of the monomials in $T=\ensuremath{\mathbb{K}}[x_0,\ldots,x_n]$ of degree $d$. Let $m_i$ be an enumeration of the monomials in $T$ of degree $d-1$. Let $t=\binom{n+d}{n}$ and $s=\binom{n+d-1}{n}$. Let $\Gamma$ be the matrix whose top $r$ rows are the values $M_j(P_i)$ of the monomials $M_j$ at the points $P_i$, and whose next (and bottom) $s$ rows are the values $(m_i\cdot M_j)(P)$, where as above the dot indicates the action of $T$ on $T$ by partial differentiation. Note that the entries of $\Gamma$ are all in $\ensuremath{\mathbb{K}}[a_0,\ldots,a_n]$. Elements in the kernel of $\Gamma$ are coefficient vectors for forms vanishing at the points $P_i$ and having a point of multiplicity $d$ at $P = a$. The assumption that there are $r=t-s-1$ points $P_i$ and that there is (up to multiplication by scalars) a unique form vanishing on the points with a point of multiplicity $m$ at $P$ means that $\Gamma$ is a $(t-1)\times t$ matrix whose rank at a general point $P$ is $t-1$. Since the entries of $\Gamma$ are monomials of degree 0 or 1, we can divide the $s$ rows having degree 1 monomials by $a_0$ and obtain a row equivalent matrix $\Gamma'$ with entries in the field $\ensuremath{\mathbb{F}}=\ensuremath{\mathbb{K}}\big(\frac{a_1}{a_0},\ldots,\frac{a_n}{a_0}\big)$. The kernel of $\Gamma'$ has dimension 1, and for any nonzero vector $v=(v_1,\ldots,v_t)$ in the kernel, we can take $F$ to be $F=\sum_iv_iM_i$. Note that $(F^*)^\circ$ (and hence $F^*$) also are in the kernel, and so can be used in place of $F$ and thus all have the same tangent cone for a general point $P=a$. Each entry of $v$ is in $\ensuremath{\mathbb{F}}$ so computing the tangent cone gives $$\sum_j \frac{((M_j\cdot F)(P))M_j}{c_j}=\sum_{i,j} \frac{((M_j\cdot v_iM_i)(P))M_j}{c_j} =\sum_i v_i\frac{((M_i\cdot M_i)(P))M_i}{c_i}=\sum_i v_iM_i=F.$$ I.e., $F$ is its own tangent cone, which for a general point $P=a$ is thus defined by $F(a,x)=0$ (or equivalently $F^*(a,x)=0$). We can also work over $R$. Let $\Gamma'^*$ be the matrix obtained by appending $(M_1,\ldots,M_t)$ as a row at the bottom of $\Gamma'$, and let $\Gamma^*$ be the matrix obtained by appending $(M_1,\ldots,M_t)$ as a row at the bottom of $\Gamma$. Then $G'=\det\Gamma'^*$ is a multiple of $F$ by a scalar in $\ensuremath{\mathbb{F}}$ and we have $a_0^sG'=G=\det \Gamma^*\in R$. Since $G'=G/a_0^s$ is a scalar multiple of $F$ by a scalar in $\ensuremath{\mathbb{F}}$, it follows that $G^*=F^*$. Moreover, we have $G=C(a)G^*$ where $C(a)$ is a polynomial describing for which points $a$ the matrix $\Gamma$ has less than full rank. (Suppose that we choose a point $a=Q_1$ such that there is a point $x=Q_2$ for which $G^*(Q_1,Q_2)\neq0$. Then $C(Q_1)=0$ if and only if $\det \Gamma^*=G(Q_1,Q_2)=0$, which occurs if and only if the maximal minors of $\Gamma$ all vanish; i.e., $\Gamma$ has rank less than $t-1$.) As before, $G$ is its own tangent cone, but it's still not clear what $F^*$ is or how $F^*(a,x)$ is related to $F^*(x,a)$. Now assume that there is an irreducible variety $W$ of degree $d$ and codimension 2 such that for a general point $P=a$ the locus $F(a,x)=0$ is precisely the union of all lines through $P$ and a point of $W$, and that $F(a,x)$ is irreducible (and hence so is $F^*(a,x)$ by Lemma \ref{StEx}). Then we have $F^*(a,x)=\pm F^*(x,a)$. Here's why. For a general point $P'=[a_0':\ldots:a_n']$ of $F(a,x)=0$ (and hence of $F^*(a,x)=0$), $P'$ is on the cone through $W$ having vertex $P$, so $P'$ is on the line through $P$ and a point $w\in W$. But then $P$ is on the line through $P'$ and $w$, so $P$ is on the cone $F(a',x)=0$ with vertex $P'$ (hence on $F^*(a',x)=0$), so $F^*(a',a)=0$. I.e., $F^*(a',a)=0$ if and only if $F^*(a,a')=0$. Thus the loci $F^*(a,x)=0$ and $F^*(x,a)=0$ intersect in a nonempty open subset of $F(a,x)=0$. Since $F^*(a,x)$ and $F^*(x,a)$ are irreducible, we have $F^*(a,x)=cF^*(x,a)$ for some scalar $c$. But swapping variables again gives $F^*(a,x)=cF^*(a,x)$ hence $F^*(a,x)=c^2F^*(a,x)$ so $c=\pm1$. Thus in this case, without resorting to Lemma \ref{StEx}(d), we see $F^*(a,x)$ has bi-degree $(d,d)$ and that the tangent cone to $F^*(a,x)$ at a general point $P=a$ is defined by $F^*(x,a)$ (since here the tangent cone is defined by $F^*(a,x)$ but $F^*(a,x)$ and $F^*(x,a)$ define the same locus).
nodes.statement_short: For the cone construction F is its own tangent cone; when F is a cone over an irreducible codimension-2 variety, F^*(a,x) = ±F^*(x,a).

nodes.name: Proof that F^*(a,x) = ±F^*(x,a) for cones
nodes.statement: Here's why. For a general point $P'=[a_0':\ldots:a_n']$ of $F(a,x)=0$ (and hence of $F^*(a,x)=0$), $P'$ is on the cone through $W$ having vertex $P$, so $P'$ is on the line through $P$ and a point $w\in W$. But then $P$ is on the line through $P'$ and $w$, so $P$ is on the cone $F(a',x)=0$ with vertex $P'$ (hence on $F^*(a',x)=0$), so $F^*(a',a)=0$. I.e., $F^*(a',a)=0$ if and only if $F^*(a,a')=0$. Thus the loci $F^*(a,x)=0$ and $F^*(x,a)=0$ intersect in a nonempty open subset of $F(a,x)=0$. Since $F^*(a,x)$ and $F^*(x,a)$ are irreducible, we have $F^*(a,x)=cF^*(x,a)$ for some scalar $c$. But swapping variables again gives $F^*(a,x)=cF^*(a,x)$ hence $F^*(a,x)=c^2F^*(a,x)$ so $c=\pm1$. Thus in this case, without resorting to Lemma \ref{StEx}(d), we see $F^*(a,x)$ has bi-degree $(d,d)$ and that the tangent cone to $F^*(a,x)$ at a general point $P=a$ is defined by $F^*(x,a)$ (since here the tangent cone is defined by $F^*(a,x)$ but $F^*(a,x)$ and $F^*(x,a)$ define the same locus).
nodes.statement_short: P' lies on the cone with vertex P iff P lies on the cone with vertex P'; irreducibility forces F^*(a,x)=cF^*(x,a), and swapping twice gives c=±1.

nodes.name: Symmetry of the cone relation
nodes.statement: Here's why. For a general point $P'=[a_0':\ldots:a_n']$ of $F(a,x)=0$ (and hence of $F^*(a,x)=0$), $P'$ is on the cone through $W$ having vertex $P$, so $P'$ is on the line through $P$ and a point $w\in W$. But then $P$ is on the line through $P'$ and $w$, so $P$ is on the cone $F(a',x)=0$ with vertex $P'$ (hence on $F^*(a',x)=0$), so $F^*(a',a)=0$.
nodes.statement_short: A point P' on the cone with vertex P puts P on the cone with vertex P'.

nodes.statement: I.e., $F^*(a',a)=0$ if and only if $F^*(a,a')=0$. Thus the loci $F^*(a,x)=0$ and $F^*(x,a)=0$ intersect in a nonempty open subset of $F(a,x)=0$.
nodes.statement_short: The two loci meet in an open subset of F(a,x)=0.

nodes.name: Power sums

nodes.name: Newton's identities

abla(e_n)$. Using Newton's identity we can rewrite this as $ rac{1}{n}

nodes.name: Bi-degree (m,m+1) of F^* for unexpected curves
nodes.statement: Let $Z\subset\ensuremath{\mathbb{P}}^2$ be a finite set of points admitting an unexpected curve $C$ of degree $m+1$ with a general point $P=[a_0:a_1:a_2]$ of multiplicity $m$. Let $F\in S$ be the form defining $C$ over the field $\ensuremath{\mathbb{K}}(\frac{a_1}{a_0},\frac{a_2}{a_0})$. Examples suggest that $F^*$ is bi-homogeneous of bi-degree $(m,m+1)$, but our proof is restricted to the case that the line arrangement dual to $Z$ is free.
nodes.statement_short: For an unexpected curve of degree m+1 with general m-fold point, F^* should always have bi-degree (m,m+1).

nodes.name: BMSS duality for unexpected plane curves
nodes.statement: Let $Z\subset\ensuremath{\mathbb{P}}^2$ be a finite set of points admitting an irreducible unexpected curve $C=C_P$ of degree $m+1$ with a general point $P=[a_0:a_1:a_2]$ of multiplicity $m$. \begin{enumerate} \item[(a)] The curve $C_P$ is unique. \item[(b)] Let $F(a,x)\in S=\ensuremath{\mathbb{K}}\big(\frac{a_1}{a_0},\frac{a_2}{a_0}\big)[x_0,x_1,x_2]$ be the form defining $C$ over the field $\ensuremath{\mathbb{K}}(\frac{a_1}{a_0},\frac{a_2}{a_0})$. Assume that the lines dual to the points of $Z$ comprise a free line arrangement. Then $F^*(a,x)$ is bi-homogeneous of bi-degree $(m,m+1)$. Furthermore, viewing $F^*(a,x) \in \ensuremath{\mathbb{K}}[x_0,x_1,x_2][a_0,a_1,a_2]$, $F^*(a,x)$ has multiplicity $m$ in the $a$ variables at the general point $[x_0:x_1:x_2]$ (briefly we will say $F^*(a,x)$ has a point of multiplicity $m$ in the $a$ variables at $a=x$). \item[(c)] Assume that $F\in R=\ensuremath{\mathbb{K}}[a_0,a_1,a_2][x_0,x_1,x_2]$ is any bi-homogeneous form of bi-degree $(m,m+1)$ such that $F(a,x)$ is reduced and irreducible for a general point $a=P$ and has multiplicity $m$ both in the $a$ variables at $a=x$ and in the $x$ variables at $x=a$. Then $F_P(a,x)=(-1)^mF(x,a)$ is the tangent cone at $x=P$ to the curve $F(P,x)=0$ for $a=P$, where $F_P$ is defined in (\ref{def of HP}). \end{enumerate}
assumptions: Let $Z\subset\ensuremath{\mathbb{P}}^2$ be a finite set of points admitting an irreducible unexpected curve $C=C_P$ of degree $m+1$ with a general point $P=[a_0:a_1:a_2]$ of multiplicity $m$.
Assume that the lines dual to the points of $Z$ comprise a free line arrangement.
conclusions: The curve $C_P$ is unique.
Then $F^*(a,x)$ is bi-homogeneous of bi-degree $(m,m+1)$.
Then $F_P(a,x)=(-1)^mF(x,a)$ is the tangent cone at $x=P$ to the curve $F(P,x)=0$ for $a=P$
nodes.statement_short: Irreducible unexpected curves are unique; for free dual arrangements F^* has bi-degree (m,m+1), and F(x,a) is (up to sign) the tangent cone at P.
