nodes.name: Proof of Theorem 4.4
nodes.statement:
(a) Since $C$ is irreducible, then \cite{CHMN} shows that $C$ is unique. (b) By Lemma ef{StEx}(d) we know that $F^*$ is bi-homogeneous of bi-degree $(m',m+1)$ for some $m'\geq m$ and that $F^*$ has multiplicity at least $m$ in the $a$ variables at $a=x$. The conclusion follows from examining a parameterization given in \cite{CHMN} to conclude that $m'\leq m$. Let $\Lambda$ be the product of the forms defining the lines dual to the points of $Z$. It is not hard to check that there are no unexpected curves for $Z$ with $|Z|<3$, so after a change of coordinates if need be, we may assume $x_0x_1$ divides $\Lambda$. Let $(s_0,s_1,s_2)$ be a syzygy of minimal degree (hence homogeneous of degree $m$; see \cite{CHMN}) for the ideal $(\Lambda_{x_0},\Lambda_{x_1},\Lambda_{x_2})$, where $\Lambda_{x_i}$ denotes the partial with respect to $x_i$; thus $$s_0\Lambda_{x_0}+s_1\Lambda_{x_1}+s_2\Lambda_{x_2}=0.$$ Define $\phi$ formally to be the vector whose components are given by the cross product $$\phi=(\phi_0,\phi_1,\phi_2)=(s_0,s_1,s_2)	imes (x_0,x_1,x_2).$$ Now let $\ell$ be the general line $a_0x_0+a_1x_1+a_2x_2=0$. If $a_2
eq0$, we can parameterize $\ell$ by $(ta_2,-a_2s,a_1s-a_0t)$, where $(t,s)$ are projective coordinates on $\ensuremath{\mathbb{P}}^1$, and by \cite{CHMN} $\phi$ defines a birational map from $\ell$ to $C$. Note that, since $x_0x_1$ divides $\Lambda$, then $x_0$ divides $\Lambda_{x_1}$ and $\Lambda_{x_2}$ and $x_1$ divides $\Lambda_{x_0}$ and $\Lambda_{x_2}$, but $x_0$ does not divide $\Lambda_{x_0}$ and $x_1$ does not divide $\Lambda_{x_1}$. Setting $x_0=0$ in $s_0\Lambda_{x_0}+s_1\Lambda_{x_1}+s_2\Lambda_{x_2}=0$ gives $$s_0\Lambda_{x_0}=0$$ so $x_0$ must divide $s_0$. Similarly, $x_1$ divides $s_1$. Plugging $(x_0,x_1,x_2)=(ta_2,-a_2s,a_1s-a_0t)$ into $\phi(x_0,x_1,x_2)$ we see from the definition of the cross product that $a_2$ divides $\phi_2(ta_2,-a_2s,a_1s-a_0t)$, and since $x_i|s_i$ for $i=0,1$, we get that $x_i$ divides $\phi_i$ for $0,1$ and thus after the substitution $(x_0,x_1,x_2)=(ta_2,-a_2s,a_1s-a_0t)$ that $a_2$ divides $\phi_i$ for $i=0,1,2$. Let $\psi_i=\phi_i/a_2$. Then $\psi_i$ is bi-homogeneous of degree $m-1$ in the $a$ variables and degree $m$ in the variables $s$ and $t$. We also get a parameterization of $C$ using the slope of lines through the point $P=a$. This induces an isomorphism from $E_P$ to $C$, where $E_P$ is the blow up of $P$. But $\psi=(\psi_0,\psi_1,\psi_2)$ induces a birational map $\ell$ to $C$. Composing gives an isomorphism $\ell$ to $E_P$, which is therefore linear. Thus after a change of coordinates fixing $P$ and $x_2=0$, we may assume that the parameterization of $C$ given by $\psi$ is the same as that given by slopes of lines through $P$. In particular, consider the line through the point $(a_1/a_2,a_1/a_2,1)$ with slope $t/s$; in affine coordinates it is $$ rac{x_1}{x_2}- rac{a_1}{a_2}= rac{t}{s}\Big( rac{x_0}{x_2}- rac{a_0}{a_2}\Big)$$ which we can rewrite as $(x_1a_2-a_1x_2)s=t(x_0a_2-a_0x_2)$. Setting $x_2=0$ gives the coordinates $a_2t=x_1, sa_2=x_0$ as the parameterization on $E_P$, and we can assume that the parameterization of $C$ given by mapping the point $(t,s)$ on $E_P$ to the point $(x_0:x_1:x_2)$ where the line $(x_1a_2-a_1x_2)s=t(x_0a_2-a_0x_2)$ meets $C$ (away from $P$) is the same point of $C$ as that given by $\psi(ta_2,-a_2s,a_1s-a_0t)$. Thus the parameterization is such that $$[x_0:x_1:x_2]=[\psi_0(ta_2,-a_2s,a_1s-a_0t):\psi_1(ta_2,-a_2s,a_1s-a_0t):\psi_2(ta_2,-a_2s,a_1s-a_0t)],$$ and hence plugging $s=x_0a_2-a_0x_2$ and $t=x_1a_2-a_1x_2$ in to $(ta_2,-a_2s,a_1s-a_0t)$ gives $(a_2(x_1a_2-a_1x_2),-a_2(x_0a_2-a_0x_2),a_1x_0a_2-a_0x_1a_2)$, and factoring out the $a_2$ we get $(x_1a_2-a_1x_2,-(x_0a_2-a_0x_2),a_1x_0-a_0x_1)$, each component of which has bi-degree $(1,1)$. So we now have parametric equations for $C$, $$[x_0:x_1:x_2]=[\psi_0(v):\psi_1(v):\psi_2(v)],$$ where $v=(x_1a_2-a_1x_2,-x_0a_2+a_0x_2,a_1x_0-a_0x_1)$, so each component of the right hand side has bi-degree $(m,m+1)$. We get the following equations for $C$ (bi-homogeneous of degree $(m,m+2)$): $x_0\psi_1-x_1\psi_0=0$, $x_0\psi_2-x_2\psi_0=0$, $x_1\psi_2-x_2\psi_1=0$. The form $F^*(a,x)$ defining $C$ is a common divisor of these three equations. Thus $F^*$ is bi-homogeneous of bi-degree $(m',m+1)$ for some $m'\leq m$. Thus $F^*$ is bi-homogeneous of bi-degree $(m,m+1)$, and since it has a point of multiplicity at least $m$ at $a=x$ but degree exactly $m$, the multiplicity is also $m$. (c) Since $F$ has degree $m$ in the $a$ variables, $F$ defines a curve of degree $m$ with a point of multiplicity $m$ at $a=x$, hence it defines a union of $m$ lines through the point $a=x$. The question remains as to what these lines are. To answer this question, translate the point $a=x$ to the point $[1:0:0]$. Doing this gives us $$G(a)=a_0^mF ig(1, rac{a_1}{a_0}+ rac{x_1}{x_0}, rac{a_2}{a_0}+ rac{x_2}{x_0},1, rac{x_1}{x_0}, rac{x_2}{x_0} ig) \in\ensuremath{\mathbb{K}}\Big[ rac{x_1}{x_0}, rac{x_2}{x_0}\Big][a_0,a_1,a_2].$$ In the $a$ variables, this defines $m$ lines meeting at $[1:0:0]$. Thus in the $a$ variables $G(a)$ is a homogeneous form of degree $m$, but now the variable $a_0$, which we can regard as defining the line at infinity, does not appear. Note that neither $a_1$ nor $a_2$ is a factor of $G(a)$, since if, say $a_1$ were a factor of $G$, then for all choices of $x$, $G=0$ includes the line from $[1:0:0]$ to $[0:0:1]$. Since the point $[0:0:1]$ is at infinity, it is fixed under the translation we employed, so $F(a_0,a_1,a_2,x_0,x_1,x_2)=0$ includes the line from $[x_0:x_1:x_2]$ to $[0:0:1]$, hence $x_1a_0-x_0a_1$ is a factor of $F$, contradicting the assumption that $C$ is irreducible. Since $a_0$ does not appear in $G(a)$ and $a_1$ and $a_2$ are not factors, we have $G(a)=b_0a_1^m+\cdots+b_ma_2^m$ with $b_i\in\ensuremath{\mathbb{K}} ig[ rac{x_1}{x_0}, rac{x_1}{x_0} ig]$ and $b_0,b_m
eq0$. Setting $a_2=1$ in $G$ gives $g(a_1)=b_0a_1^m+\cdots+b_m$ and dividing by $b_0$ gives $h(a_1)=g(a_1)/b_0\in\ensuremath{\mathbb{K}}( rac{x_1}{x_0}, rac{x_1}{x_0})[a_1]$. Over an appropriate field extension of $\ensuremath{\mathbb{K}}( rac{x_1}{x_0}, rac{x_1}{x_0})$ this factors as $h(a_1)=(a_1-h_1)\cdots(a_1-h_m)$. Note that the elements $h_i$ are distinct. If not, then $h$ and hence $g$ has a multiple root, say $h_i$, hence $a_1-h_i$ is a common factor of $g$ and $g'$ (or, taking more derivatives, of $g^{(\mu-1)}$ and $g^{(\mu)}$ if the root has multiplicity $\mu>1$) and thus can be found using the Euclidean algorithm. Thus the linear factor $a_1-h_i$ is in $\ensuremath{\mathbb{K}}( rac{x_1}{x_0}, rac{x_1}{x_0})[a_1]$ and so divides $g$ over $\ensuremath{\mathbb{K}}( rac{x_1}{x_0}, rac{x_1}{x_0})[a_1]$ and hence $a_1-h_ia_2$ divides $G(a)$ in $\ensuremath{\mathbb{K}} ig[ rac{x_1}{x_0}, rac{x_1}{x_0} ig][a_0,a_1,a_2]$ and thus $F(a,x)$ as before has a corresponding factor linear in $a$, contrary to assumption. Thus the roots $h_i$ are distinct. Since by Lemma ef{diffMap} the mapping $f$ expressing the coefficients of $h$ as symmetric functions of the roots $h_i$ has an invertible differential $df$ (the roots being distinct), we can by the inverse function theorem \cite[p.\ 33]{FG} regard the roots $h_i$ as holomorphic functions of the coefficients $b_i/b_0$ of $h$. Since each $b_i/b_0$ is a rational (and so holomorphic) function of $x_1/x_0$ and $x_2/x_0$, we can regard the $h_i$ as holomorphic functions of $x_1/x_0$ and $x_2/x_0$. The roots $h_i$ give the points at infinity where $G(a,x)$ vanishes. Specifically these are $[0:h_i:1]$. These are unaffected by affine translations, so the points where $F(a,x)$ vanishes on $a_0=0$ are these same points $[0:h_i:1]$. Thus translating back we see $F(a,x)$ vanishes on the lines through $[x_0:x_1:x_2]$ and $[0:h_i:1]$, so the forms defining these lines divide $F(a,x)$. Specifically, we have $G(a)=b_0(a_1-h_1a_2)\cdots(a_1-h_ma_2)$ so $$b_0\Big( rac{a_1}{a_0}-h_1 rac{a_2}{a_0}\Big)\cdots\Big( rac{a_1}{a_0}-h_m rac{a_2}{a_0}\Big)=G(a)/a_0^m= F\Big(1, rac{a_1}{a_0}+ rac{x_1}{x_0}, rac{a_2}{a_0}+ rac{x_2}{x_0},1, rac{x_1}{x_0}, rac{x_2}{x_0}\Big)$$ translates back to $$F(a,x)=x_0^{m+1}a_0^mb_0\Big( rac{a_1}{a_0}- rac{x_1}{x_0}- ig( rac{a_2}{a_0}- rac{x_2}{x_0} ig)h_1\Big)\cdots \Big( rac{a_1}{a_0}- rac{x_1}{x_0}- ig( rac{a_2}{a_0}- rac{x_2}{x_0} ig)h_m\Big)=$$ $$x_0b_0 ig((a_1x_0-a_0x_1)-(a_2x_0-a_0x_2)h_1 ig)\cdots  ig((a_1x_0-a_0x_1)-(a_2x_0-a_0x_2)h_m ig)=$$ $$b_0x_0\left| egin{array} {ccc} 0 & h_1(x) & 1\ x_0 & x_1 & x_2\ a_0 & a_1 & a_2\ \end{array} ight|\cdots \left| egin{array} {ccc} 0 & h_m(x) & 1\ x_0 & x_1 & x_2\ a_0 & a_1 & a_2\ \end{array} ight|.$$ Consider a point $x=a$ where $b_0x_0
eq0$. Then the branches of $F(a,x)=0$ in a neighborhood of $x=a$ are defined by the vanishing of each factor $\lambda_i(x_0,x_1,x_2)=\left| egin{array} {ccc} 0 & h_i(x) & 1\ x_0 & x_1 & x_2\ a_0 & a_1 & a_2\ \end{array} ight|$. The tangent line to the branch $\lambda_i(x)=0$ at $x=a$ is defined by $((
abla \lambda_i)|_{x=a})\cdot (x_0,x_1,x_2)$. Since $\lambda_i=(a_1-a_2h_i)x_0-a_0x_1+a_0x_2h_i$, the gradient $
abla \lambda_i$ is $$\Big((a_1-a_2h_i),-a_0,a_0h_i\Big)+\Big(-a_2h_{i0}x_0+a_0x_2h_{i0},-a_2h_{i1}x_0+a_0x_2h_{i1},-a_2h_{i2}x_0+a_0x_2h_{i2}\Big).$$ The second term vanishes at $x=a$ so $$(
abla \lambda_i)|_{x=a}\cdot(x_0,x_1,x_2)=(a_1-a_2h_i(x),-a_0,a_0h_i(x))|_{x=a}\cdot(x_0,x_1,x_2)=\left| egin{array} {ccc} 0 & h_i(a) & 1\ x_0 & x_1 & x_2\ a_0 & a_1 & a_2\ \end{array} ight|.$$ So we see that the tangent cone to $F(a,x)=0$ at a point $P=a$ such that $b_0x_0
eq0$ is defined by the vanishing of $$F_P(a,x)=b_0(a)a_0\left| egin{array} {ccc} 0 & h_1(a) & 1\ x_0 & x_1 & x_2\ a_0 & a_1 & a_2\ \end{array} ight|\cdots \left| egin{array} {ccc} 0 & h_m(a) & 1\ x_0 & x_1 & x_2\ a_0 & a_1 & a_2\ \end{array} ight|=$$ $$(-1)^mb_0(a)a_0\left| egin{array} {ccc} 0 & h_1(a) & 1\ a_0 & a_1 & a_2\ x_0 & x_1 & x_2\ \end{array} ight|\cdots \left| egin{array} {ccc} 0 & h_m(a) & 1\ a_0 & a_1 & a_2\ x_0 & x_1 & x_2\ \end{array} ight|=(-1)^mF(x,a).$$

nodes.name: BMSS duality for unique unexpected curves
nodes.statement: Let $Z\subset\ensuremath{\mathbb{P}}^2$ be a finite set of points admitting a unique unexpected curve $C$ of degree $m+1$ with a general point $P=[a_0:a_1:a_2]$ of multiplicity $m$. Let $F(a,x)\in S$ be the form defining $C$ over the field $\ensuremath{\mathbb{K}}(\frac{a_1}{a_0},\frac{a_2}{a_0})$ and assume $F^*$ is bi-homogeneous of bi-degree $(m,m+1)$. Then $(F^*)_P(a,x)=(-1)^mF^*(x,a)$ defines the tangent cone to $C$ at $P$.
assumptions: Let $Z\subset\ensuremath{\mathbb{P}}^2$ be a finite set of points admitting a unique unexpected curve $C$ of degree $m+1$ with a general point $P=[a_0:a_1:a_2]$ of multiplicity $m$.
assume $F^*$ is bi-homogeneous of bi-degree $(m,m+1)$.
conclusions: Then $(F^*)_P(a,x)=(-1)^mF^*(x,a)$ defines the tangent cone to $C$ at $P$.
nodes.label: BMSSDualityCor

nodes.name: Proof of Corollary 4.5
nodes.statement: It is shown in \cite{CHMN} that $C=C'\cup \Lambda_1\cup\cdots\cup \Lambda_r$ where $C'$ is unexpected for a subset $Z'$ of $Z$ and has degree $m+1-r$ with a general point $P$ of multiplicity $m-r$ where $r=|Z|-|Z'|$ and each $\Lambda_i$ is the line from $P$ to $p_i$ where $p_1,\ldots, p_r$ are the points of $Z$ not in $Z'$. Thus $F=GL_1\cdots L_r$, where $G$ is the form defining $C'$ and $L_i$ is the bi-linear form defining $\Lambda_i$. So we have $F^*=G^*L_1^*\cdots L_r^*$, but $L_i^*=L_i$ and $L_i(a,x)=-L_(x,a)$, so $F^*(a,x)=(G^*L_1\cdots L_r)(a,x)=(-1)^m(G^*L_1\cdots L_r)(x,a)$. The tangent cone for $C$ is the tangent cone for $C'$ union with the lines $L_i$, so we also see that $(-1)^mG^*(x,a)L_1^*(x,a)\cdots L_r^*(x,a)=F^*(x,a)$ defines the tangent cone for $C$.
nodes.statement_short: Decompose C into an irreducible unexpected part and lines through P (CHMN); each factor satisfies the duality.

nodes.name: The B3 unexpected quartic
nodes.statement: The form $F(a,x)$ defining the unexpected quartic curve $C$ for the $B_3$ configuration is $$F(a,x)=a_2^3x_0^3x_1-a_2^3x_0x_1^3-a_1^3x_0^3x_2+(3a_0a_1^2-3a_0a_2^2)x_0^2x_1x_2+ (-3a_0^2a_1+3a_1a_2^2)x_0x_1^2x_2+a_0^3x_1^3x_2+$$ $$(3a_0^2a_2-3a_1^2a_2)x_0x_1x_2^2+a_1^3x_0x_2^3-a_0^3x_1x_2^3=$$ $$(x_1^3x_2-x_1x_2^3)a_0^3-3x_0x_1^2x_2a_0^2a_1+3x_0^2x_1x_2a_0a_1^2+(-x_0^3x_2+x_0x_2^3)a_1^3+3x_0x_1x_2^2a_0^2a_2$$ $$-3x_0x_1x_2^2a_1^2a_2-3x_0^2x_1x_2a_0a_2^2+3x_0x_1^2x_2a_1a_2^2+(x_0^3x_1-x_0x_1^3)a_2^3.$$ Substituting $a_0=x_0=1$ and restricting to the line $L$ defined by $x_1=a_1$ gives $$F(1,a_1,a_2,1,a_1,x_2)=a_1(a_1^2-1)(x_2-a_2)^3,$$ while substituting $a_0=x_0=1,a_1=x_1$ gives $$F(1,x_1,a_2,1,x_1,x_2)=x_1(x_1^2-1)(x_2-a_2)^3.$$ Thus we see that $F$ has a triple point both in terms of the $a$ variables and the $x$ variables. To see that the factors of $F(x,a)$ are just the lines tangent to the branches of $F(a,x)$, one can graph $F(a,x)$ and $F(x,a)$ on the same coordinate axes; see Figure \ref{TCFig}.
nodes.statement_short: Explicit F(a,x) for the B3 quartic: a triple point both in a and in x; F(x,a) gives the tangent lines at the triple point.
nodes.label: QuarticUnexpCurveEx

nodes.name: Irreducible unexpected curves from non-free arrangements
nodes.statement: The line arrangement of lines dual to the 9 points of $Z$ giving the irreducible unexpected curve in Example \ref{QuarticUnexpCurveEx} (i.e., the $B_3$ arrangement of 9 lines) is free. This raises the question of whether every irreducible unexpected curve comes from a free arrangement. It is not true that irreducible unexpected curves never come from non-free line arrangements. For example, consider Figure \ref{20lines} (which comes from \cite[Example 6.2]{CHMN}); it gives a non-free arrangement of 19 lines (these 19 being the 18 solid lines shown in the figure plus the line at infinity). The 19 points dual to these 19 lines gives a set of points $Z$ having an irreducible unexpected curve of degree 9 with a general point of multiplicity 8. However, by including the dotted line shown in the figure, we obtain a free arrangement of 20 lines for which the dual set $Z'$ of 20 points has the same unexpected curve.
nodes.statement_short: A non-free 19-line arrangement has an irreducible unexpected curve; adding one line makes it free with the same curve.
nodes.label: unexpNotFree

nodes.name: BMSS duality for non-free arrangements
nodes.statement: Suppose $Z$ is a finite set of points which admits an unexpected curve of degree $d=m+1$ having a general point $P$ of multiplicity $m$. If the arrangement of lines dual to $Z$ is not free, to what extent does BMSS duality still hold?

nodes.name: BMSS duality in higher dimensions
nodes.statement: To what extent does BMSS duality hold in higher dimensions? For example, it holds for $B_4$ and $F_4$ with $d=m=4$. In these cases the unexpected surfaces are defined by a form $F(a,x)$ of bi-degree $(4,4)$ and the form for the tangent cone at $P$ is $F(x,a)$. It also holds for $D_4$ with $d=m=3$. In this case the unexpected surfaces are defined by a form $F(a,x)$ of bi-degree $(3,3)$ and the form for the tangent cone at $P$ is $-F(x,a)$.

nodes.name: Associated base locus
nodes.statement: Given an unexpected variety for a finite point set $Z$ having a general point $P$ of multiplicity $m$ and degree $d$, let $B_Z(P)$ be the base locus of $[I_{Z+mP}]_d$ and let $B_Z=\cap_P B_Z(P)$, which we can refer to as the base locus associated to $Z$. What can be said about this associated base locus? For example, what is its dimension? If it is 0-dimensional, when is it strictly larger than $Z$?

nodes.name: Which root systems have unexpected hypersurfaces
nodes.statement: What is special about the root systems having unexpected hypersurfaces? For example, why do the systems $A_{n+1}$ not seem to have any?

nodes.name: Unexpected hypersurfaces for B_{n+1}
nodes.statement: For the systems $B_{n+1}$, computational runs suggest there might be unexpected hypersurfaces with $d=m=4$ for all $n\geq 3$ and for $d=m=3$ for all $n\geq5$. How can one prove this? And why only $3\leq m\leq 4$?

nodes.name: Role of the syzygy bundle in higher dimension
nodes.statement: Is there a class of finite sets of points in $\ensuremath{\mathbb{P}}^n$ for $n \geq 3$ (or respectively a condition on $(d,m)$) for which the syzygy bundle plays a similar role, in the study of unexpected hypersurfaces, to that which it plays when $n=2$ and $m = d-1$, or is that purely a phenomenon for the plane?

nodes.name: Bi-degree of F^* for 2m+2 points
nodes.statement: Let $Z$ be a set of points in $\ensuremath{\mathbb{P}}^2$ admitting a (unique) unexpected curve of degree $m+1$ with a general point of multiplicity $m$. Then $Z + mP$ does not impose independent conditions on forms of degree $m+1$, but for a suitable subset $Z'$ of $2m+2$ of the points of $Z$, $Z' + mP$ does impose independent conditions, and the curve is still unique (but it is no longer unexpected for $Z'$). So suppose we consider more generally sets $Z$ of $2m+2$ points such that there is a unique irreducible curve of degree $m+1$ containing $Z$ and having a general point of multiplicity $m$ (but not necessarily unexpected). How does the bi-degree of $F^*$ depend on $Z$? Is there a connection between this bi-degree and the question of whether $Z$ extends to a set of points for which the curve is unexpected?

nodes.name: Extending to free arrangements
nodes.statement: Suppose $Z\subset\ensuremath{\mathbb{P}}^2$ is a finite set of points having an irreducible unexpected curve where (as in Remark \ref{unexpNotFree}) the arrangement of lines dual to $Z$ is not free. Is it true that there is a finite set $Z'$ with $Z\subset Z'\subset\ensuremath{\mathbb{P}}^2$ such that $Z'$ has the same unexpected curve as does $Z$ but such that the arrangement of lines dual to $Z'$ is free?

nodes.name: Uniqueness, then set-up for unexpectedness
nodes.statement: We first check uniqueness. Let $F$ be a form defining a surface containing $C$, of degree $d$ with multiplicity $d$ at $P$. Let $\lambda$ be a line through $P$ and any point $Q$, of $C$. Then by B\'ezout, $F$ must vanish on all of $\lambda$. Thus the surface defined by $F$ is precisely $S_P$. We now check unexpectedness. Let $D$ be a smooth plane curve of degree $d$.
nodes.statement_short: Prove uniqueness and introduce a smooth plane curve D for comparison.

nodes.name: Uniqueness via Bezout
nodes.statement: We first check uniqueness. Let $F$ be a form defining a surface containing $C$, of degree $d$ with multiplicity $d$ at $P$. Let $\lambda$ be a line through $P$ and any point $Q$, of $C$. Then by B\'ezout, $F$ must vanish on all of $\lambda$. Thus the surface defined by $F$ is precisely $S_P$.
nodes.statement_short: Bezout forces any such surface to contain every line PQ, so it is S_P.

nodes.name: Introduce plane curve D
nodes.statement: We now check unexpectedness. Let $D$ be a smooth plane curve of degree $d$.
nodes.statement_short: Compare C with a smooth plane curve D of the same degree.

nodes.name: Claim 1: genus bound
nodes.statement: \underline{Claim 1}: {\em The arithmetic genus, $g_C$, of $C$ is strictly less than that of $D$, which is $g_D = \binom{d-1}{2}$. } \medskip This argument is classical. Much of it is given in \cite{harris} (when C is irreducible) and in \cite{migbook} Proposition 1.4.2, so no claim is made to originality; we include it here just for the reader's convenience. Let $\Gamma$ be a general hyperplane section of $C$ by a hyperplane $H$ defined by a general linear form $L$. Let $I_{\Gamma | H}$ be the saturated ideal of $\Gamma$ in $H$. Let $\ell \gg 0$. Then \[ \begin{array}{rcl} d\ell - g_C + 1 & = & h^0(\mathcal O_C(\ell)) \\ & = & h_{R/I_C}(\ell) \end{array} \] where $h_{R/I_C}(t)$ is the Hilbert function of $C$. On the other hand, for any integer $t$ we have the exact sequence \[ \begin{array}{ccccccccccccccccccc} 0 & \rightarrow & [I_C]_{t-1} & \rightarrow & [I_C]_t & \rightarrow & [I_{\Gamma|H} ]_t & \longrightarrow & H^1(\mathcal I_C(t-1)) & \rightarrow & \dots \\ &&&&&&\hbox{\ \ \ \ \ \ \ } \searrow & & \nearrow \hbox{\ \ \ \ \ \ \ \ \ \ \ \ } \\ &&&&&&& [K]_t \\ &&&&&&\hbox{\ \ \ \ \ \ \ } \nearrow & & \searrow \hbox{\ \ \ \ \ \ \ \ \ \ \ \ } \\ &&&&&&\hbox{\ } 0 & & 0 \hbox{\ \ \ \ \ \ } \\ \end{array} \] (where $K$ is just the cokernel). Then after adding and subtracting some binomial coefficients and setting $\bar R = R/L$, we obtain \[ \begin{array}{rcl} \Delta h_{R/I_C} (t) & = & h_{\bar R/I_{\Gamma|H}}(t) + \dim [K]_t \\ & \geq & h_{\bar R/I_{\Gamma | H}} (t). \end{array} \] So since $\ell \gg 0$ we obtain \[ \begin{array}{rcl} g_C & = & 1 + d\ell - h_{R/I_C}(\ell) \\ & = & d\ell - \sum_{t=1}^\ell \Delta h_{R/I_C}(t) \\ & \leq & d\ell - \sum_{t=1}^\ell h_{\bar R/I_{\Gamma|H}} (t) \\ & = & \sum_{t=1}^\ell \left [ d - h_{\bar R/I_{\Gamma | H}} (t) \right ]. \end{array} \] Now replace $C$ by $D$, and replace $\Gamma$ by the hyperplane section of $D$, which is a set of $d$ collinear points, say $A$. We have, similarly, \[ g_D = \sum_{t=1}^\ell \left [ d - h_{\bar R/I_A}(t) \right ] = \binom{d-1}{2} . \] It is clear that for any $t \geq 1$ we have \[ h_{\bar R/I_{\Gamma|H}} (t) \geq h_{\bar R/I_A}(t) \] with strict inequality for $t=1$, so we obtain $g_C < g_D$. This completes the proof of Claim 1.
nodes.statement_short: Show g_C < g_D = binom(d-1,2).

nodes.name: Attribution
nodes.statement: This argument is classical. Much of it is given in \cite{harris} (when C is irreducible) and in \cite{migbook} Proposition 1.4.2, so no claim is made to originality; we include it here just for the reader's convenience.
nodes.statement_short: The argument is classical (Harris; Migliore).

nodes.name: Hyperplane section and Hilbert polynomial
nodes.statement: Let $\Gamma$ be a general hyperplane section of $C$ by a hyperplane $H$ defined by a general linear form $L$. Let $I_{\Gamma | H}$ be the saturated ideal of $\Gamma$ in $H$. Let $\ell \gg 0$. Then \[ \begin{array}{rcl} d\ell - g_C + 1 & = & h^0(\mathcal O_C(\ell)) \\ & = & h_{R/I_C}(\ell) \end{array} \] where $h_{R/I_C}(t)$ is the Hilbert function of $C$.
nodes.statement_short: Take a general hyperplane section Γ; express the Hilbert function at large ℓ via the genus.

nodes.name: Difference bound
nodes.statement: On the other hand, for any integer $t$ we have the exact sequence \[ \begin{array}{ccccccccccccccccccc} 0 & \rightarrow & [I_C]_{t-1} & \rightarrow & [I_C]_t & \rightarrow & [I_{\Gamma|H} ]_t & \longrightarrow & H^1(\mathcal I_C(t-1)) & \rightarrow & \dots \\ &&&&&&\hbox{\ \ \ \ \ \ \ } \searrow & & \nearrow \hbox{\ \ \ \ \ \ \ \ \ \ \ \ } \\ &&&&&&& [K]_t \\ &&&&&&\hbox{\ \ \ \ \ \ \ } \nearrow & & \searrow \hbox{\ \ \ \ \ \ \ \ \ \ \ \ } \\ &&&&&&\hbox{\ } 0 & & 0 \hbox{\ \ \ \ \ \ } \\ \end{array} \] (where $K$ is just the cokernel). Then after adding and subtracting some binomial coefficients and setting $\bar R = R/L$, we obtain \[ \begin{array}{rcl} \Delta h_{R/I_C} (t) & = & h_{\bar R/I_{\Gamma|H}}(t) + \dim [K]_t \\ & \geq & h_{\bar R/I_{\Gamma | H}} (t). \end{array} \]
nodes.statement_short: Restriction sequence gives Δh_C(t) >= h_Γ(t).

nodes.name: Genus bound for C
nodes.statement: So since $\ell \gg 0$ we obtain \[ \begin{array}{rcl} g_C & = & 1 + d\ell - h_{R/I_C}(\ell) \\ & = & d\ell - \sum_{t=1}^\ell \Delta h_{R/I_C}(t) \\ & \leq & d\ell - \sum_{t=1}^\ell h_{\bar R/I_{\Gamma|H}} (t) \\ & = & \sum_{t=1}^\ell \left [ d - h_{\bar R/I_{\Gamma | H}} (t) \right ]. \end{array} \]
nodes.statement_short: Sum to bound g_C by sum of d - h_Γ(t).

nodes.name: Genus of D
nodes.statement: Now replace $C$ by $D$, and replace $\Gamma$ by the hyperplane section of $D$, which is a set of $d$ collinear points, say $A$. We have, similarly, \[ g_D = \sum_{t=1}^\ell \left [ d - h_{\bar R/I_A}(t) \right ] = \binom{d-1}{2} . \]
nodes.statement_short: The same computation for D with d collinear points gives g_D = binom(d-1,2).

nodes.name: Compare
nodes.statement: It is clear that for any $t \geq 1$ we have \[ h_{\bar R/I_{\Gamma|H}} (t) \geq h_{\bar R/I_A}(t) \] with strict inequality for $t=1$, so we obtain $g_C < g_D$. This completes the proof of Claim 1.
nodes.statement_short: Non-collinear Γ has larger Hilbert function, so g_C < g_D.

nodes.name: Cohomology vanishing
nodes.statement: Now, by \cite{GLP} Remark (1) (p. 497), we have $H^1(\mathcal I_C(d)) = H^2(\mathcal I_C(d)) = 0$, and we also have $H^1(\mathcal I_D(d)) = H^2(\mathcal I_D(d)) = 0$. Consider the exact sequence \[ 0 \rightarrow [I_C]_d \rightarrow H^0(\mathcal O_{\ensuremath{\mathbb{P}}^3}(d)) \rightarrow H^0(\mathcal O_C(d)) \rightarrow H^1(\mathcal I_C(d)) \rightarrow 0. \]
nodes.statement_short: Gruson-Lazarsfeld-Peskine gives H^1, H^2 vanishing in degree d.

nodes.name: Claim 2: h^0 comparison
nodes.statement: \underline{Claim 2}: {\em Let $D$ be a plane curve of degree $d$. Then $h^0(\mathcal O_C(d)) > h^0(\mathcal O_D(d))$.} \medskip Indeed, \[ \begin{array}{rcl} d^2 - g_C + 1 & = & h^0(\mathcal O_C(d)) - h^1(\mathcal O_C(d)) \\ & = & h^0(\mathcal O_C(d)) - h^2(\mathcal I_C(d)) \\ & = & h^0(\mathcal O_C(d)) \end{array} \] and similarly for $D$, so thanks to Claim 1 we have \[ h^0(\mathcal O_C(d)) > h^0(\mathcal O_D(d)) \] and we have Claim 2.
nodes.statement_short: Riemann-Roch with Claim 1 gives h^0(O_C(d)) > h^0(O_D(d)).

nodes.name: Bound dim[I_C]_d
nodes.statement: Then \[ \begin{array}{rcll} \dim [I_C]_d & = & \displaystyle \binom{d+3}{3} - h^0(\mathcal O_C(d)) & \hbox{(since } h^1(\mathcal I_C(d)) = 0 ) \\ \\ & < & \displaystyle \binom{d+3}{3} - h^0(\mathcal O_D(d)) \end{array} \] thanks to Claim 2.
nodes.statement_short: dim[I_C]_d < binom(d+3,3) - h^0(O_D(d)).

nodes.name: Conclude unexpectedness
nodes.statement: To check that $S_P$ is an unexpected surface it is enough to note that \[ \begin{array}{rcl} \displaystyle \dim [I_C]_d - \binom{d-1+3}{3} & < & \displaystyle \binom{d+3}{3} - h^0(\mathcal O_D(d)) - \binom{d-1+3}{3} \\ \\ & = & \displaystyle \binom{d+2}{2} - [d^2 - g_D + 1] \\ \\ & = & 1 \end{array} \] using the value of $g_D$ mentioned above.
nodes.statement_short: Expected dimension is < 1, so the cone is unexpected.

nodes.name: Restriction sequence
nodes.statement: We have the exact sequence \[ 0 \rightarrow [I_V]_0 \rightarrow [I_V]_1 \rightarrow [I_{W|H}]_1 \rightarrow H^1(\mathcal I_V (0)) \rightarrow \dots \] We want to show that the third vector space in this exact sequence is zero.
nodes.statement_short: Reduce to vanishing of [I_{W|H}]_1.

nodes.name: Non-degeneracy of V
nodes.statement: But $[I_V]_1 = 0$ since $V$ is non-degenerate.

nodes.name: Claim: H^1(I_V(0)) = 0
nodes.statement: On the other hand, we claim that $H^1(\mathcal I_V(0)) = 0$. This will complete the proof. But we also have the exact sequence \[ 0 \rightarrow [I_V]_0 \rightarrow [R]_0 \rightarrow H^0(\mathcal O_V(0)) \rightarrow H^1(\mathcal I_V(0)) \rightarrow 0. \] The first term is clearly zero. The second has dimension 1. The third has dimension 1 since $V$ is connected (being of codimension 2 and equidimensional) and reduced (by hypothesis). Thus the claim follows.
nodes.statement_short: Show H^1(I_V(0)) vanishes, completing the proof.

nodes.name: Second exact sequence
nodes.statement: But we also have the exact sequence \[ 0 \rightarrow [I_V]_0 \rightarrow [R]_0 \rightarrow H^0(\mathcal O_V(0)) \rightarrow H^1(\mathcal I_V(0)) \rightarrow 0. \]
nodes.statement_short: Use the sequence 0 → [I_V]_0 → [R]_0 → H^0(O_V) → H^1(I_V(0)) → 0.

nodes.name: Dimension count
nodes.statement: The first term is clearly zero. The second has dimension 1. The third has dimension 1 since $V$ is connected (being of codimension 2 and equidimensional) and reduced (by hypothesis). Thus the claim follows.
nodes.statement_short: V connected and reduced gives h^0(O_V)=1, so H^1 vanishes.

nodes.name: Base case
nodes.statement: The proof is by induction on $n$. The initial case is Proposition \ref{cone in P3}, so we can assume $n \geq 4$.
nodes.statement_short: Induction on n; base case is Proposition 2.1.

nodes.name: Inductive hypothesis on a hyperplane section
nodes.statement: Let $H$ be a general hyperplane through $P$ and let $W = V \cap H$. Since $P$ is general, we can assume that $H$ is general as well. By Lemma \ref{nondeg}, $W$ is non-degenerate in $H = \ensuremath{\mathbb{P}}^{n-1}$, and it is also reduced and equidimensional. Let $T_P$ be the cone in $H$ over $W$ with vertex $P$. Thus by induction, $T_P$ is the unique hypersurface of degree $d$ containing $W$ with multiplicity $d$ at $P$, and it is unexpected.
nodes.statement_short: By Lemma 2.3 and induction, the cone T_P over W = V∩H is unique and unexpected in H.

nodes.name: Dimension formula
nodes.statement: Consider the exact sequence \[ \begin{array}{ccccccccccccccccccc} 0 & \rightarrow & [I_V]_{d-1} & \rightarrow & [I_V]_d & \rightarrow & [I_{W|H} ]_d & \longrightarrow & H^1(\mathcal I_V(d-1)) & \rightarrow & \dots \\ &&&&&&\hbox{\ \ \ \ \ \ \ } \searrow & & \nearrow \hbox{\ \ \ \ \ \ \ \ \ \ \ \ } \\ &&&&&&& [K]_d \\ &&&&&&\hbox{\ \ \ \ \ \ \ } \nearrow & & \searrow \hbox{\ \ \ \ \ \ \ \ \ \ \ \ } \\ &&&&&&\hbox{\ } 0 & & 0 \hbox{\ \ \ \ \ \ } \\ \end{array} \] We have \[ \dim [I_V]_d = \dim [I_V]_{d-1} + \dim [I_{W|H}]_d - \dim [K]_d. \]
nodes.statement_short: Exact sequence gives dim[I_V]_d in terms of degree d-1 and the section.

nodes.name: Claim: dim[I_V]_d - binom(d-1+n,n) <= 0
nodes.statement: We claim that \[ \dim [I_V]_d - \binom{d-1+n}{n} \leq 0 \] so that $S_P$ is unexpected. We have \[ \begin{array}{rcl} \displaystyle \dim [I_V]_d - \binom{d-1+n}{n} & = & \displaystyle \dim [I_V]_{d-1} + \left ( \dim [I_{W|H}]_d - \binom{d-1+(n-1)}{n-1} \right ) \\ \\ && \displaystyle + \binom{d-1+(n-1)}{n-1} - \dim [K]_d - \binom{d-1+n}{n} \\ \\ & \leq & \displaystyle \dim [I_V]_{d-1} + \binom{d+n-2}{n-1} - \dim [K]_d - \binom{d+n-1}{n} \\ \\ & = & \displaystyle \dim [I_V]_{d-1} - \binom{d+n-2}{n} - \dim [K]_d . \end{array} \] But Remark \ref{low deg rmk} gives \[ \dim [I_V]_{d-1} \leq \binom{d+n-2}{n}, \] which completes the claim.
nodes.statement_short: Show the expected dimension is non-positive.

nodes.name: Rewrite the difference
nodes.statement: We have \[ \begin{array}{rcl} \displaystyle \dim [I_V]_d - \binom{d-1+n}{n} & = & \displaystyle \dim [I_V]_{d-1} + \left ( \dim [I_{W|H}]_d - \binom{d-1+(n-1)}{n-1} \right ) \\ \\ && \displaystyle + \binom{d-1+(n-1)}{n-1} - \dim [K]_d - \binom{d-1+n}{n} \\ \\ & \leq & \displaystyle \dim [I_V]_{d-1} + \binom{d+n-2}{n-1} - \dim [K]_d - \binom{d+n-1}{n} \\ \\ & = & \displaystyle \dim [I_V]_{d-1} - \binom{d+n-2}{n} - \dim [K]_d . \end{array} \]
nodes.statement_short: Bound using unexpectedness of T_P.

nodes.name: Apply Remark 2.2
nodes.statement: But Remark \ref{low deg rmk} gives \[ \dim [I_V]_{d-1} \leq \binom{d+n-2}{n}, \] which completes the claim.
nodes.statement_short: dim[I_V]_{d-1} <= binom(d+n-2,n).

nodes.name: Uniqueness
nodes.statement: Uniqueness follows in the same way as it did for Proposition~\ref{cone in P3}.
nodes.statement_short: Uniqueness as in Proposition 2.1.

nodes.name: Goal inequality
nodes.statement: Let $Y = C \cup kP$. We want to show that \begin{equation} \max \left\{ 0 , \dim[I_C]_k - \binom{k+2}{3} \right\} < \dim [I_Y]_k. \end{equation}
nodes.statement_short: Set Y = C ∪ kP and state inequality (2.1).

nodes.name: Compute expected dimension
nodes.statement: Modifying the calculation above, we know that \[ \dim [I_C]_k = \binom{k+3}{3} - [dk - g_C + 1] \] so \[ \dim [I_C]_k - \binom{k+2}{3} = \binom{k+2}{2} - dk + g_C -1. \]
nodes.statement_short: dim[I_C]_k from Riemann-Roch.

nodes.name: Lower bound from multiples of the cone
nodes.statement: On the other hand, we have a unique surface $S_P$ of degree $d$ with a singularity of multiplicity $d$ at the general point $P$, so by multiplying $S_P$ by an element of $[I_P^{k-d}]_{k-d}$ we always obtain a surface of degree $k$ with multiplicity $k$ at $P$. Thus \[ \dim [I_Y]_k \geq \binom{k-d+2}{2}, \] in particular $\dim [I_Y]_k > 0$.
nodes.statement_short: Multiplying S_P by forms of I_P^{k-d} gives dim[I_Y]_k >= binom(k-d+2,2).

nodes.name: Reduction
nodes.statement: Thus combining, it is enough to show \[ \binom{k+2}{2} - dk + g_C -1 < \binom{k-d+2}{2}. \]
nodes.statement_short: Reduce to a numerical inequality.

nodes.name: Genus bound
nodes.statement: A calculation shows that this is equivalent to \[ g_C < \frac{(d-1)(d-2)}{2}, \] which we showed in Claim 1 of Proposition \ref{cone in P3}.
nodes.statement_short: Equivalent to g_C < (d-1)(d-2)/2, i.e. Claim 1.

nodes.name: Reduce to V
nodes.statement: Let $F$ be the form defining $S$. Then \[ [I_Z]_{d+e} = [I_Y]_{d+e} = F \cdot [I_V]_d \] so \[ \dim [I_Z]_{d+e} - \binom{d+n-1}{n} = \dim [I_V]_d - \binom{d+n-1}{n} < 1 \] as we saw in the proof of Proposition \ref{Pn}.
nodes.statement_short: [I_Z]_{d+e} = F·[I_V]_d, so the count is as for V.

nodes.name: Conclude
nodes.statement: Thus $S_P \cup S$ is an unexpected hypersurface of degree $d+e$ with a singular point of multiplicity $d$ at $P$.
nodes.statement_short: S_P ∪ S is unexpected.

nodes.name: Degree m+1 cases
nodes.statement: For (i), we first note that there is an unexpected curve of degree $m+1$ and multiplicity $m$ at a general point for each $m \geq 3$. Indeed,
nodes.statement_short: Show unexpected curves of degree m+1 exist for each m>=3.

nodes.name: Case m<=2
nodes.statement: $m \leq 2$. It was shown by Akesseh \cite{A} that this occurs only in characteristic 2. (See also \cite{FGST} for a different proof that shows that it does not occur in characteristic zero.)
nodes.statement_short: Akesseh: only in characteristic 2.

nodes.name: Case m=3
nodes.statement: $m=3$. This comes from the dual of the $B_3$ arrangement \cite{DIV}.
nodes.statement_short: Dual of the B3 arrangement.

nodes.name: Case m=4
nodes.statement: $m=4$. Consider the line arrangement defined by the linear factors of $$xyz(x^3-y^3)(x^3-z^3)(y^3-z^3).$$ This is a supersolvable arrangement (see definition in \S\ref{root system section}), so Theorem 3.7 of \cite{DMO} applies. In particular, the dual points give a reduced set of 12 points which admit an unexpected curve with $d=5$ and $m=4$.
nodes.statement_short: A supersolvable arrangement of 12 lines via Di Marca-Malara-Oneto.

nodes.name: Case m=5
nodes.statement: $m=5$. This follows from \cite{CHMN} Proposition 6.15, taking $k=2$.
nodes.statement_short: CHMN Proposition 6.15.

nodes.name: Case m>=6
nodes.statement: $m \geq 6$. This comes from the points dual to the Fermat arrangement, by \cite{CHMN} Proposition 6.15, taking $t \geq 5$.
nodes.statement_short: Fermat arrangement via CHMN Proposition 6.15.

nodes.name: d = m impossible in the plane
nodes.statement: It is clear that a set of points $Z$ in $\ensuremath{\mathbb{P}}^2$ cannot admit an unexpected curve whose degree and multiplicity at a general point $P$ are equal (unlike what we have seen in $\ensuremath{\mathbb{P}}^3$). Indeed, in this situation the line joining $P$ to any point of $Z$ must be a component of such an unexpected curve, so the unexpected curve is a cone with vertex $P$ over the points of $Z$. Let $d = \deg Z$ be the degree of this curve. Then $Z$ imposes independent conditions on curves of degree $d$, so $\dim [I_Z]_d = \binom{d+2}{2} - d$. Then \[ \dim [I_Z]_d - \binom{(d-1)+2}{2} = \binom{d+2}{2} - d - \binom{d+1}{2} = (d+1)-d = 1 \] so in fact the cone is not unexpected. Thus $m < d$.
nodes.statement_short: A cone over points in P^2 is never unexpected, so m<d.

nodes.name: Add a curve A
nodes.statement: With this preparation, we use the same argument as was used to prove Corollary \ref{add S}. Let $Z_0$ be a set of points admitting an unexpected curve of degree $m+1$ and multiplicity $m$ at a general point $P$ and let $A$ be a plane curve of degree $d-m-1$ not passing through any point of $Z_0$. Since $P$ is general, it does not lie on $A$. Then choosing sufficiently many points on $A$ gives a unique unexpected curve of degree $d$ and multiplicity $m$ at $P$. (A similar construction also was used in \cite[Proposition 6.7]{DIV}, but see \cite[Example 7.4]{CHMN}.)
nodes.statement_short: Add a curve A of degree d-m-1 to Z_0 and many points on A, as in Corollary 2.14.

nodes.name: Part (ii)
nodes.statement: Part (ii) follows from Proposition \ref{Pn} and Corollary \ref{add S}.
nodes.statement_short: From Proposition 2.4 and Corollary 2.14.

nodes.name: Multiplication sequence
nodes.statement: Let $L$ be a general linear form. Consider the exact sequence \begin{equation} \dots \rightarrow [R/(L_1^d, \dots, L_{r}^d)]_{m-1} \stackrel{\times L^{d-m+1}}{\longrightarrow} [R/(L_1^{d},\dots,L_{r}^{d})]_{d} \rightarrow [R/(L_1^{d},\dots,L_{r}^{d},L^{d-m+1})]_{d} \rightarrow 0. \end{equation}
nodes.statement_short: Exact sequence of multiplication by L^{d-m+1}.

nodes.name: Macaulay duality
nodes.statement: Let $P$ be the general point of $\ensuremath{\mathbb{P}}^n$ dual to $L$. By Macaulay duality \cite{EI} and exactness, \[ \begin{array}{rcl} \dim [I_Z \cap I_P^{m}]_{d} & = & \dim [R/(L_1^{d} , \dots, L_r^{d},L^{d-m+1})]_{d} \\ \\ & \geq & \dim [R/(L_1^d,\dots, L_r^d)]_d - \dim [R/(L_1^d,\dots,L_r^d)]_{m-1} \\ \\ & = & \displaystyle \dim [I_Z]_d - \binom{n+m-1}{n}. \end{array} \]
nodes.statement_short: Macaulay duality identifies dim[I_Z ∩ I_P^m]_d with the cokernel dimension.

nodes.name: Compare conditions
nodes.statement: Since (a) holds if and only if $\dim [I_Z \cap I_P^{m}]_{d}>\max(0, \dim [I_Z]_d - \binom{n+m-1}{n})$ if and only if $\dim [R/(L_1^{d} , \dots, L_r^{d},L^{d-m+1})]_{d}>\max(0, \dim [R/(L_1^d,\dots, L_r^d)]_d - \dim [R/(L_1^d,\dots,L_r^d)]_{m-1})$ if and only if (b) holds, the result follows.
nodes.statement_short: Unexpectedness is exactly a cokernel larger than expected.

nodes.name: Apply Corollary 2.12
nodes.statement: The statement about linear general position is immediate since $C$ is reduced, irreducible and non-degenerate. From Corollary \ref{higher deg} we know that $C$ has an unexpected surface of degree $k$ with a general point $P$ of multiplicity $k$, so we have $\dim [I_C \cap I_P^k]_k>\max(0,\dim [I_C]_k - \binom{k+2}{3})$.
nodes.statement_short: C has an unexpected surface of degree k with k-fold general point.

nodes.name: Transfer to Z and to WLP
nodes.statement: But by B\'ezout's theorem we have $[I_Z]_k = [I_C]_k$ so we obtain $\dim [I_Z \cap I_P^k]_k>\max(0,\dim [I_Z]_k - \binom{k+2}{3})$, hence $Z$ has an unexpected surface of degree $k$ with multiplicity $k$ at $P$, so $R/(L_1^k,\dots,L_m^k)$ fails the WLP in degree $k-1$ by Proposition \ref{SLPvUH}.
nodes.statement_short: Bezout gives [I_Z]_k=[I_C]_k; Proposition 2.17 gives failure of WLP.

nodes.name: Existence of V
nodes.statement: We recall that we can always find an irreducible, non-degenerate subvariety $V$ of codimension 2 and degree $k$ in $\ensuremath{\mathbb{P}}^n$.
nodes.statement_short: Recall an irreducible non-degenerate codimension-2 V of degree k exists.

nodes.name: Construct V
nodes.statement: In fact, if $k$ is even we take $V$ as an intersection of a general form of degree $\frac{k}{2}$ and a general quadric. If $k$ is odd we take $V$ as a general arithmetically Cohen-Macaulay subscheme with a minimal free resolution of the form \[ 0 \rightarrow R(- {\textstyle \frac{k+3}{2} })^2 \rightarrow R(- {\textstyle \frac{k+1}{2} })^2 \oplus R(-2) \rightarrow R \rightarrow R/I_V \rightarrow 0 \] (obtained, for example, by linking from a linear space of codimension 2 using the complete intersection of a quadric and a form of degree $\frac{k+1}{2}$).
nodes.statement_short: Complete intersection for even k; linked ACM scheme for odd k.

nodes.name: Hilbert function of V
nodes.statement: Using this sequence, or the Koszul resolution if $k$ is even, we obtain \[ \dim [R/I_V]_k = f (n, k). \]
nodes.statement_short: dim[R/I_V]_k = f(n,k).

nodes.name: General points on V
nodes.statement: Since $V$ is irreducible, it makes sense to speak of a general set of points on $V$. Let $Z$ be a general set of $N$ points on $V$. From the generality of $Z$ we have \[ \dim [R/I_Z]_k = \min \{ \dim [R/I_V]_k , |Z| \}, \] hence $\dim [I_V]_k = \dim [I_Z]_k$.
nodes.statement_short: N general points on V have the same degree-k forms as V.

nodes.name: Apply Proposition 2.4
nodes.statement: By Proposition 2.4 we then have that the cone over $V$ with vertex at a general point $P$ is an unexpected hypersurface of degree $k$ and multiplicity $k$ at $P$.
nodes.statement_short: The cone over V is unexpected.

nodes.name: Failure of maximal rank
nodes.statement: Then the argument in the proof of Corollary 2.16 can be extended to our situation to show that the multiplication from degree $k-1$ to degree $k$ by a general linear form has an unexpectedly large cokernel, i.e. maximal rank does not hold.
nodes.statement_short: As in the earlier WLP corollary, the cokernel is unexpectedly large.

nodes.name: Linear general position
nodes.statement: Since $Z$ is general on $V$ and $V$ is irreducible and non-degenerate, $Z$ is a set of points in linear general position, and this implies the condition on the linear forms not to have a common zero.
nodes.statement_short: General points on V are in linear general position.

nodes.name: Part (a)
nodes.statement: (a) Since $F=BF^*/H=B(F^*)^\circ a_0^t/H$, where $t=\deg(H)-\deg(B)$, we see that $F$ and $(F^*)^\circ$ differ by $Ba_0^t/H$, which is a unit in $S$.
nodes.statement_short: F and (F^*)° differ by a unit.

nodes.name: Part (b)
nodes.statement: (b) Note that $F$ and $(F^*)^\circ$ differ by a unit factor in $S$, so one is irreducible if and only if the other is. Also, $F^*$ by construction has no factors of bi-degree $(f,0)$ with $f>0$, so if $F^*$ fails to be irreducible, it factors as $F^*=AB$ where $A$ and $B$ have bi-degree $(a,d_A)$ and $(b,d_B)$ with $d_A,d_B>0$ and $d_A+d_B=d$. But then $(F^*)^\circ=A^\circ B^\circ$ is a product of factors of positive degree and hence not irreducible.
nodes.statement_short: A factorization of F^* would give one of (F^*)°.

nodes.name: Part (c)
nodes.statement: (c) If $G^\circ$ is not irreducible, then $G^\circ=AB$ where both $A$ and $B$ have positive degree $d_A$ and $d_B$, so we have $G=\alpha A^*\beta B^*$ where $A^*$ and $B^*$ have bi-degrees $(a,d_A)$ and $(b,d_B)$, and $\alpha$ and $\beta$ have bi-degrees $(t_\alpha,0)$ and $(t_\beta,0)$. Since $R$ is a UFD, the denominators in the right hand side of the expression $G=\alpha A^*\beta B^*$ must cancel with factors of the numerators of the expression $\alpha A^*\beta B^*$ and this does not affect the values of $d_A$ or $d_B$, so we may assume that $\alpha,\beta, A^*, B^*$ all are in $R$ and $A^*$ and $B^*$ have bi-degrees $(a',d_A)$ and $(b',d_B)$, where the simplification might have changed $a$ and $b$ but will have left $d_a$ and $d_B$ unchanged. Since $d_A$ and $d_B$ are both positive, $G$ has nonunit factors so $G$ is not irreducible. Now note that irreducibility of $G^\circ$ implies that for $(G^\circ)^*$ by (b). Finally, by construction, if $G$ is irreducible with bi-degree $(t,d)$ where $d>0$, then $G=c(G^\circ)^*$ for some nonzero $c\in\ensuremath{\mathbb{K}}$, hence $(G)=((G^\circ)^*)$.
nodes.statement_short: Factor G° and lift via UFD property of R.

nodes.name: Part (d)
nodes.statement: (d) Since $F\in I_{mP}$, by (a) we have $\frac{F^*}{a_0^s}=(F^*)^\circ\in I_{mP}$, where $(s,d)$ is the bi-degree of $F^*$, and since $d$ is the degree of $(F^*)^\circ$ and since $(F^*)^\circ\in I_{mP}$ we have $d\geq m$. Now let $$D\big(\frac{a_1}{a_0},\ldots,\frac{a_n}{a_0},\frac{x_1}{x_0},\ldots,\frac{x_n}{x_0}\big)= F^*\big(\frac{a_0}{a_0},\ldots,\frac{a_n}{a_0},\frac{x_0}{x_0},\frac{x_1}{x_0},\ldots,\frac{x_n}{x_0}\big)=\frac{F^*(a_0,\ldots,a_n,x_0,\ldots,x_n)}{a_0^sx_0^d},$$ so as a rational function $D$ has bi-degree $(0,0)$, but as a polynomial in $\ensuremath{\mathbb{K}}(\frac{a_1}{a_0},\ldots,\frac{a_n}{a_0})[\frac{x_1}{x_0},\ldots,\frac{x_n}{x_0}]$, $D$ has degree $\delta\leq d$. Moreover, since $x_0\not\in I_P$, we have $D\in I_{mQ}$ where $Q$ is the point $Q=(\frac{a_1}{a_0},\ldots,\frac{a_n}{a_0})$ in the affine open subset $\ensuremath{\mathbb{K}}(\frac{a_1}{a_0},\ldots,\frac{a_n}{a_0})^n$ away from $x_0=0$. Now translate $Q$ to the origin; i.e., consider $$H\big(\frac{a_1}{a_0},\ldots,\frac{a_n}{a_0},\frac{x_1}{x_0},\ldots,\frac{x_n}{x_0}\big)= D\big(\frac{a_1}{a_0},\ldots,\frac{a_n}{a_0},\frac{x_1}{x_0}+\frac{a_1}{a_0},\ldots,\frac{x_n}{x_0}+\frac{a_n}{a_0}\big).$$ Note that $$a_0^{s+d}x_0^dH=a_0^{s+d}x_0^dF^*\big(\frac{a_0}{a_0},\ldots,\frac{a_n}{a_0},\frac{x_0}{x_0},\frac{x_1}{x_0}+\frac{a_1}{a_0},\ldots,\frac{x_n}{x_0}+\frac{a_n}{a_0}\big)=$$ $$F^*\big(a_0,\ldots,a_n,a_0x_0,a_0x_1+a_1x_0,\ldots,a_0x_n+a_nx_0\big)\in R$$ is a bi-homogeneous polynomial of bi-degree $(s+d,d)$. Since $H$ has multiplicity $m$ at the origin (with respect to the variables $\frac{x_1}{x_0},\ldots,\frac{x_n}{x_0}$), $H$ is a sum of terms where each term consists of a monomial in $\frac{x_1}{x_0},\ldots,\frac{x_n}{x_0}$ of degree at least $m$ and at most $d$, times a polynomial in the variables $\frac{a_1}{a_0},\ldots,\frac{a_n}{a_0}$ of degree at most $s+d$. Thus each term is of the form $$c\big(\frac{a_1}{a_0},\ldots,\frac{a_n}{a_0}\big)\big(\frac{x_1}{x_0}\big)^{i_1}\cdots\big(\frac{x_n}{x_0}\big)^{i_n}$$ where $m\leq \sum_ji_j\leq d$ and $c$ has degree at most $s+d$. Thus multiplying by $a_0^{s+d}x_0^d$ clears the denominators. Translating back we recover $D$; i.e., $$D\big(\frac{a_1}{a_0},\ldots,\frac{a_n}{a_0},\frac{x_1}{x_0},\ldots,\frac{x_n}{x_0}\big)= H\big(\frac{a_1}{a_0},\ldots,\frac{a_n}{a_0},\frac{x_1}{x_0}-\frac{a_1}{a_0},\ldots,\frac{x_n}{x_0}-\frac{a_n}{a_0}\big),$$ but each term becomes $$c\big(\frac{a_1}{a_0},\ldots,\frac{a_n}{a_0}\big)\big(\frac{x_1}{x_0}-\frac{a_1}{a_0}\big)^{i_1}\cdots\big(\frac{x_n}{x_0}-\frac{a_n}{a_0}\big)^{i_n} =c\big(\frac{a_1}{a_0},\ldots,\frac{a_n}{a_0}\big)\big(\frac{a_0x_1-a_1x_0}{a_0x_0}\big)^{i_1}\cdots\big(\frac{a_0x_n-a_nx_0}{a_0x_0}\big)^{i_n}$$ and multiplying by $a_0^{2d+s}x_0^d$ we obtain $$C(a_0,\ldots,a_n)(a_0x_1-a_1x_0)^{i_1}\cdots(a_0x_n-a_nx_0)^{i_n}$$ where $C$ is homogeneous in the variables $a_i$ of degree $s+d$, and $$(a_0x_1-a_1x_0)^{i_1}\cdots(a_0x_n-a_nx_0)^{i_n}\in J_{mP}.$$ Thus $a_0^{2d+s}x_0^dH\big(\frac{a_1}{a_0},\ldots,\frac{a_n}{a_0},\frac{x_1}{x_0}-\frac{a_1}{a_0},\ldots,\frac{x_n}{x_0}-\frac{a_n}{a_0}\big)= a_0^{2d+s}x_0^dD=a_0^{2d}F^*\in J_{mP}$. But by \cite[Corollary 7.10]{BV}, since $J_P$ is the ideal generated by the maximal minors of a $2 \times (n+1)$ matrix of indeterminates, namely the two sets of variables, the powers $J_{mP}$ are primary for $J_P$. Since no power of $a_0$ is in $J_{mP}$, we see that $F^*\in J_{mP}$.
nodes.statement_short: Show F^* lies in J_{mP}.

nodes.name: Degree bound
nodes.statement: (d) Since $F\in I_{mP}$, by (a) we have $\frac{F^*}{a_0^s}=(F^*)^\circ\in I_{mP}$, where $(s,d)$ is the bi-degree of $F^*$, and since $d$ is the degree of $(F^*)^\circ$ and since $(F^*)^\circ\in I_{mP}$ we have $d\geq m$.
nodes.statement_short: By (a), (F^*)° is in I_{mP}, so d>=m.

nodes.name: Dehomogenize and translate
nodes.statement: Now let $$D\big(\frac{a_1}{a_0},\ldots,\frac{a_n}{a_0},\frac{x_1}{x_0},\ldots,\frac{x_n}{x_0}\big)= F^*\big(\frac{a_0}{a_0},\ldots,\frac{a_n}{a_0},\frac{x_0}{x_0},\frac{x_1}{x_0},\ldots,\frac{x_n}{x_0}\big)=\frac{F^*(a_0,\ldots,a_n,x_0,\ldots,x_n)}{a_0^sx_0^d},$$ so as a rational function $D$ has bi-degree $(0,0)$, but as a polynomial in $\ensuremath{\mathbb{K}}(\frac{a_1}{a_0},\ldots,\frac{a_n}{a_0})[\frac{x_1}{x_0},\ldots,\frac{x_n}{x_0}]$, $D$ has degree $\delta\leq d$. Moreover, since $x_0\not\in I_P$, we have $D\in I_{mQ}$ where $Q$ is the point $Q=(\frac{a_1}{a_0},\ldots,\frac{a_n}{a_0})$ in the affine open subset $\ensuremath{\mathbb{K}}(\frac{a_1}{a_0},\ldots,\frac{a_n}{a_0})^n$ away from $x_0=0$. Now translate $Q$ to the origin; i.e., consider $$H\big(\frac{a_1}{a_0},\ldots,\frac{a_n}{a_0},\frac{x_1}{x_0},\ldots,\frac{x_n}{x_0}\big)= D\big(\frac{a_1}{a_0},\ldots,\frac{a_n}{a_0},\frac{x_1}{x_0}+\frac{a_1}{a_0},\ldots,\frac{x_n}{x_0}+\frac{a_n}{a_0}\big).$$ Note that $$a_0^{s+d}x_0^dH=a_0^{s+d}x_0^dF^*\big(\frac{a_0}{a_0},\ldots,\frac{a_n}{a_0},\frac{x_0}{x_0},\frac{x_1}{x_0}+\frac{a_1}{a_0},\ldots,\frac{x_n}{x_0}+\frac{a_n}{a_0}\big)=$$ $$F^*\big(a_0,\ldots,a_n,a_0x_0,a_0x_1+a_1x_0,\ldots,a_0x_n+a_nx_0\big)\in R$$ is a bi-homogeneous polynomial of bi-degree $(s+d,d)$.
nodes.statement_short: Dehomogenize F^* to D and translate Q to the origin to get H.

nodes.name: Expand H
nodes.statement: Since $H$ has multiplicity $m$ at the origin (with respect to the variables $\frac{x_1}{x_0},\ldots,\frac{x_n}{x_0}$), $H$ is a sum of terms where each term consists of a monomial in $\frac{x_1}{x_0},\ldots,\frac{x_n}{x_0}$ of degree at least $m$ and at most $d$, times a polynomial in the variables $\frac{a_1}{a_0},\ldots,\frac{a_n}{a_0}$ of degree at most $s+d$. Thus each term is of the form $$c\big(\frac{a_1}{a_0},\ldots,\frac{a_n}{a_0}\big)\big(\frac{x_1}{x_0}\big)^{i_1}\cdots\big(\frac{x_n}{x_0}\big)^{i_n}$$ where $m\leq \sum_ji_j\leq d$ and $c$ has degree at most $s+d$. Thus multiplying by $a_0^{s+d}x_0^d$ clears the denominators.
nodes.statement_short: H is a sum of monomials of degree between m and d.

nodes.name: Translate back
nodes.statement: Translating back we recover $D$; i.e., $$D\big(\frac{a_1}{a_0},\ldots,\frac{a_n}{a_0},\frac{x_1}{x_0},\ldots,\frac{x_n}{x_0}\big)= H\big(\frac{a_1}{a_0},\ldots,\frac{a_n}{a_0},\frac{x_1}{x_0}-\frac{a_1}{a_0},\ldots,\frac{x_n}{x_0}-\frac{a_n}{a_0}\big),$$ but each term becomes $$c\big(\frac{a_1}{a_0},\ldots,\frac{a_n}{a_0}\big)\big(\frac{x_1}{x_0}-\frac{a_1}{a_0}\big)^{i_1}\cdots\big(\frac{x_n}{x_0}-\frac{a_n}{a_0}\big)^{i_n} =c\big(\frac{a_1}{a_0},\ldots,\frac{a_n}{a_0}\big)\big(\frac{a_0x_1-a_1x_0}{a_0x_0}\big)^{i_1}\cdots\big(\frac{a_0x_n-a_nx_0}{a_0x_0}\big)^{i_n}$$ and multiplying by $a_0^{2d+s}x_0^d$ we obtain $$C(a_0,\ldots,a_n)(a_0x_1-a_1x_0)^{i_1}\cdots(a_0x_n-a_nx_0)^{i_n}$$ where $C$ is homogeneous in the variables $a_i$ of degree $s+d$, and $$(a_0x_1-a_1x_0)^{i_1}\cdots(a_0x_n-a_nx_0)^{i_n}\in J_{mP}.$$ Thus $a_0^{2d+s}x_0^dH\big(\frac{a_1}{a_0},\ldots,\frac{a_n}{a_0},\frac{x_1}{x_0}-\frac{a_1}{a_0},\ldots,\frac{x_n}{x_0}-\frac{a_n}{a_0}\big)= a_0^{2d+s}x_0^dD=a_0^{2d}F^*\in J_{mP}$.
nodes.statement_short: Each term becomes a product of the generators a_0x_j - a_jx_0, so a_0^{2d}F^* is in J_{mP}.

nodes.name: Primary powers
nodes.statement: But by \cite[Corollary 7.10]{BV}, since $J_P$ is the ideal generated by the maximal minors of a $2 \times (n+1)$ matrix of indeterminates, namely the two sets of variables, the powers $J_{mP}$ are primary for $J_P$. Since no power of $a_0$ is in $J_{mP}$, we see that $F^*\in J_{mP}$.
nodes.statement_short: Powers of J_P are J_P-primary (Bruns-Vetter), so F^* is in J_{mP}.

nodes.name: Part (e)
nodes.statement: (e) If $G\in J_{mP}$, then $G=\sum_s H_sM_s$ where each $M_s$ is a product of $m$ forms such as $a_ix_j-a_jx_i$ and each $H_s$ is a bi-homogeneous form of bi-degree $(t-m,d-m)$. So $G^\circ$ is obtained by dividing $G$ by $a_0^t$, hence we get $G^\circ=\sum_s H_s^\circ M_s^\circ$, and each $M_s^\circ$ is a product of $m$ forms such as $(a_ix_j-a_jx_i)/a_0$, each of which is in $I_P$. Thus $G^\circ\in I_{mP}$.
nodes.statement_short: Generators of J_P map into I_P.

nodes.name: Strategy
nodes.statement: The proof is to show by applying row operations involving multiplying rows by $-1$ and adding multiples of one row to another that one obtains the Vandermonde matrix.
nodes.statement_short: Row-reduce df to the Vandermonde matrix.

nodes.name: Apply Newton's identities
nodes.statement:
Row $n$ of the matrix $df$ is the gradient of $e_n$, namely $
abla(e_n)$. Using Newton's identity we can rewrite this as $ rac{1}{n}
abla(\sum_{j=1}^n(-1)^{j-1}e_{n-j}p_j)= rac{1}{n}\sum_{j=1}^n(-1)^{j-1}(
abla(e_{n-j})p_j+e_{n-j}
abla(p_j))$. Using row operations, we can (up to row equivalence) clear out the terms $
abla(e_{n-j})p_j$ since these are multiples of rows $
abla(e_i)$ higher up in the matrix. We can do the same now for row $n-1$, and then row $n-2$, etc.

nodes.statement:
Afterward, row 1 is unchanged (it is $

abla(p_1)-
abla(p_2))$, so we can use row 1 to clear the term $e_1
abla(p_1)$ so that row 2 becomes $-
abla(p_2)$, at which point we can use rows 1 and 2 to clear row 3 so that row 3 becomes $
abla(p_3)$. Continuing in this way we eventually obtain a matrix row equivalent to $df$ whose rows are $
abla(p_1)=(1,\ldots,1)$, $- rac{1}{2}
abla(p_2)=-(x_1,\cdots,x_n)$, $\ldots$, $(-1)^{n-1} rac{1}{n}
abla(p_n)=(-1)^{n-1}(x_1^{n-1},\cdots,x_n^{n-1})$. Up to sign, this is the Vandermonde matrix, whose determinant is well known to be as claimed.
nodes.statement_short: Rows become ±(1/i)∇p_i, the Vandermonde matrix.

nodes.name: Part (a)
nodes.statement: (a) Since $C$ is irreducible, then \cite{CHMN} shows that $C$ is unique.
nodes.statement_short: CHMN uniqueness.

nodes.name: Part (b)
nodes.statement: (b) By Lemma \ref{StEx}(d) we know that $F^*$ is bi-homogeneous of bi-degree $(m',m+1)$ for some $m'\geq m$ and that $F^*$ has multiplicity at least $m$ in the $a$ variables at $a=x$. The conclusion follows from examining a parameterization given in \cite{CHMN} to conclude that $m'\leq m$. Let $\Lambda$ be the product of the forms defining the lines dual to the points of $Z$. It is not hard to check that there are no unexpected curves for $Z$ with $|Z|<3$, so after a change of coordinates if need be, we may assume $x_0x_1$ divides $\Lambda$. Let $(s_0,s_1,s_2)$ be a syzygy of minimal degree (hence homogeneous of degree $m$; see \cite{CHMN}) for the ideal $(\Lambda_{x_0},\Lambda_{x_1},\Lambda_{x_2})$, where $\Lambda_{x_i}$ denotes the partial with respect to $x_i$; thus $$s_0\Lambda_{x_0}+s_1\Lambda_{x_1}+s_2\Lambda_{x_2}=0.$$ Define $\phi$ formally to be the vector whose components are given by the cross product $$\phi=(\phi_0,\phi_1,\phi_2)=(s_0,s_1,s_2)\times (x_0,x_1,x_2).$$ Now let $\ell$ be the general line $a_0x_0+a_1x_1+a_2x_2=0$. If $a_2\neq0$, we can parameterize $\ell$ by $(ta_2,-a_2s,a_1s-a_0t)$, where $(t,s)$ are projective coordinates on $\ensuremath{\mathbb{P}}^1$, and by \cite{CHMN} $\phi$ defines a birational map from $\ell$ to $C$. Note that, since $x_0x_1$ divides $\Lambda$, then $x_0$ divides $\Lambda_{x_1}$ and $\Lambda_{x_2}$ and $x_1$ divides $\Lambda_{x_0}$ and $\Lambda_{x_2}$, but $x_0$ does not divide $\Lambda_{x_0}$ and $x_1$ does not divide $\Lambda_{x_1}$. Setting $x_0=0$ in $s_0\Lambda_{x_0}+s_1\Lambda_{x_1}+s_2\Lambda_{x_2}=0$ gives $$s_0\Lambda_{x_0}=0$$ so $x_0$ must divide $s_0$. Similarly, $x_1$ divides $s_1$. Plugging $(x_0,x_1,x_2)=(ta_2,-a_2s,a_1s-a_0t)$ into $\phi(x_0,x_1,x_2)$ we see from the definition of the cross product that $a_2$ divides $\phi_2(ta_2,-a_2s,a_1s-a_0t)$, and since $x_i|s_i$ for $i=0,1$, we get that $x_i$ divides $\phi_i$ for $0,1$ and thus after the substitution $(x_0,x_1,x_2)=(ta_2,-a_2s,a_1s-a_0t)$ that $a_2$ divides $\phi_i$ for $i=0,1,2$. Let $\psi_i=\phi_i/a_2$. Then $\psi_i$ is bi-homogeneous of degree $m-1$ in the $a$ variables and degree $m$ in the variables $s$ and $t$. We also get a parameterization of $C$ using the slope of lines through the point $P=a$. This induces an isomorphism from $E_P$ to $C$, where $E_P$ is the blow up of $P$. But $\psi=(\psi_0,\psi_1,\psi_2)$ induces a birational map $\ell$ to $C$. Composing gives an isomorphism $\ell$ to $E_P$, which is therefore linear. Thus after a change of coordinates fixing $P$ and $x_2=0$, we may assume that the parameterization of $C$ given by $\psi$ is the same as that given by slopes of lines through $P$. In particular, consider the line through the point $(a_1/a_2,a_1/a_2,1)$ with slope $t/s$; in affine coordinates it is $$\frac{x_1}{x_2}-\frac{a_1}{a_2}=\frac{t}{s}\Big(\frac{x_0}{x_2}-\frac{a_0}{a_2}\Big)$$ which we can rewrite as $(x_1a_2-a_1x_2)s=t(x_0a_2-a_0x_2)$. Setting $x_2=0$ gives the coordinates $a_2t=x_1, sa_2=x_0$ as the parameterization on $E_P$, and we can assume that the parameterization of $C$ given by mapping the point $(t,s)$ on $E_P$ to the point $(x_0:x_1:x_2)$ where the line $(x_1a_2-a_1x_2)s=t(x_0a_2-a_0x_2)$ meets $C$ (away from $P$) is the same point of $C$ as that given by $\psi(ta_2,-a_2s,a_1s-a_0t)$. Thus the parameterization is such that $$[x_0:x_1:x_2]=[\psi_0(ta_2,-a_2s,a_1s-a_0t):\psi_1(ta_2,-a_2s,a_1s-a_0t):\psi_2(ta_2,-a_2s,a_1s-a_0t)],$$ and hence plugging $s=x_0a_2-a_0x_2$ and $t=x_1a_2-a_1x_2$ in to $(ta_2,-a_2s,a_1s-a_0t)$ gives $(a_2(x_1a_2-a_1x_2),-a_2(x_0a_2-a_0x_2),a_1x_0a_2-a_0x_1a_2)$, and factoring out the $a_2$ we get $(x_1a_2-a_1x_2,-(x_0a_2-a_0x_2),a_1x_0-a_0x_1)$, each component of which has bi-degree $(1,1)$. So we now have parametric equations for $C$, $$[x_0:x_1:x_2]=[\psi_0(v):\psi_1(v):\psi_2(v)],$$ where $v=(x_1a_2-a_1x_2,-x_0a_2+a_0x_2,a_1x_0-a_0x_1)$, so each component of the right hand side has bi-degree $(m,m+1)$. We get the following equations for $C$ (bi-homogeneous of degree $(m,m+2)$): $x_0\psi_1-x_1\psi_0=0$, $x_0\psi_2-x_2\psi_0=0$, $x_1\psi_2-x_2\psi_1=0$. The form $F^*(a,x)$ defining $C$ is a common divisor of these three equations. Thus $F^*$ is bi-homogeneous of bi-degree $(m',m+1)$ for some $m'\leq m$. Thus $F^*$ is bi-homogeneous of bi-degree $(m,m+1)$, and since it has a point of multiplicity at least $m$ at $a=x$ but degree exactly $m$, the multiplicity is also $m$.
nodes.statement_short: Bound the a-degree of F^* by m via a parameterization.

nodes.name: Lower bound and strategy
nodes.statement: (b) By Lemma \ref{StEx}(d) we know that $F^*$ is bi-homogeneous of bi-degree $(m',m+1)$ for some $m'\geq m$ and that $F^*$ has multiplicity at least $m$ in the $a$ variables at $a=x$. The conclusion follows from examining a parameterization given in \cite{CHMN} to conclude that $m'\leq m$.
nodes.statement_short: Lemma 3.1(d): bi-degree (m',m+1) with m'>=m; aim to show m'<=m.

nodes.name: Minimal syzygy and φ
nodes.statement: Let $\Lambda$ be the product of the forms defining the lines dual to the points of $Z$. It is not hard to check that there are no unexpected curves for $Z$ with $|Z|<3$, so after a change of coordinates if need be, we may assume $x_0x_1$ divides $\Lambda$. Let $(s_0,s_1,s_2)$ be a syzygy of minimal degree (hence homogeneous of degree $m$; see \cite{CHMN}) for the ideal $(\Lambda_{x_0},\Lambda_{x_1},\Lambda_{x_2})$, where $\Lambda_{x_i}$ denotes the partial with respect to $x_i$; thus $$s_0\Lambda_{x_0}+s_1\Lambda_{x_1}+s_2\Lambda_{x_2}=0.$$ Define $\phi$ formally to be the vector whose components are given by the cross product $$\phi=(\phi_0,\phi_1,\phi_2)=(s_0,s_1,s_2)\times (x_0,x_1,x_2).$$
nodes.statement_short: Take a minimal-degree syzygy of the Jacobian ideal and its cross product φ with x.

nodes.name: Parameterize a general line
nodes.statement: Now let $\ell$ be the general line $a_0x_0+a_1x_1+a_2x_2=0$. If $a_2\neq0$, we can parameterize $\ell$ by $(ta_2,-a_2s,a_1s-a_0t)$, where $(t,s)$ are projective coordinates on $\ensuremath{\mathbb{P}}^1$, and by \cite{CHMN} $\phi$ defines a birational map from $\ell$ to $C$.
nodes.statement_short: φ maps the general line ℓ birationally onto C (CHMN).

nodes.name: Divisibility of syzygy
nodes.statement: Note that, since $x_0x_1$ divides $\Lambda$, then $x_0$ divides $\Lambda_{x_1}$ and $\Lambda_{x_2}$ and $x_1$ divides $\Lambda_{x_0}$ and $\Lambda_{x_2}$, but $x_0$ does not divide $\Lambda_{x_0}$ and $x_1$ does not divide $\Lambda_{x_1}$. Setting $x_0=0$ in $s_0\Lambda_{x_0}+s_1\Lambda_{x_1}+s_2\Lambda_{x_2}=0$ gives $$s_0\Lambda_{x_0}=0$$ so $x_0$ must divide $s_0$. Similarly, $x_1$ divides $s_1$.
nodes.statement_short: x_i divides s_i for i=0,1.

nodes.name: Define ψ
nodes.statement: Plugging $(x_0,x_1,x_2)=(ta_2,-a_2s,a_1s-a_0t)$ into $\phi(x_0,x_1,x_2)$ we see from the definition of the cross product that $a_2$ divides $\phi_2(ta_2,-a_2s,a_1s-a_0t)$, and since $x_i|s_i$ for $i=0,1$, we get that $x_i$ divides $\phi_i$ for $0,1$ and thus after the substitution $(x_0,x_1,x_2)=(ta_2,-a_2s,a_1s-a_0t)$ that $a_2$ divides $\phi_i$ for $i=0,1,2$. Let $\psi_i=\phi_i/a_2$. Then $\psi_i$ is bi-homogeneous of degree $m-1$ in the $a$ variables and degree $m$ in the variables $s$ and $t$.
nodes.statement_short: a_2 divides φ_i after substitution; ψ = φ/a_2 has bi-degree (m-1,m).

nodes.name: Match with slope parameterization
nodes.statement: We also get a parameterization of $C$ using the slope of lines through the point $P=a$. This induces an isomorphism from $E_P$ to $C$, where $E_P$ is the blow up of $P$. But $\psi=(\psi_0,\psi_1,\psi_2)$ induces a birational map $\ell$ to $C$. Composing gives an isomorphism $\ell$ to $E_P$, which is therefore linear. Thus after a change of coordinates fixing $P$ and $x_2=0$, we may assume that the parameterization of $C$ given by $\psi$ is the same as that given by slopes of lines through $P$. In particular, consider the line through the point $(a_1/a_2,a_1/a_2,1)$ with slope $t/s$; in affine coordinates it is $$\frac{x_1}{x_2}-\frac{a_1}{a_2}=\frac{t}{s}\Big(\frac{x_0}{x_2}-\frac{a_0}{a_2}\Big)$$ which we can rewrite as $(x_1a_2-a_1x_2)s=t(x_0a_2-a_0x_2)$. Setting $x_2=0$ gives the coordinates $a_2t=x_1, sa_2=x_0$ as the parameterization on $E_P$, and we can assume that the parameterization of $C$ given by mapping the point $(t,s)$ on $E_P$ to the point $(x_0:x_1:x_2)$ where the line $(x_1a_2-a_1x_2)s=t(x_0a_2-a_0x_2)$ meets $C$ (away from $P$) is the same point of $C$ as that given by $\psi(ta_2,-a_2s,a_1s-a_0t)$.
nodes.statement_short: After a coordinate change, ψ agrees with the parameterization by slopes of lines through P.

nodes.name: Bi-degree (m,m+1)
nodes.statement: Thus the parameterization is such that $$[x_0:x_1:x_2]=[\psi_0(ta_2,-a_2s,a_1s-a_0t):\psi_1(ta_2,-a_2s,a_1s-a_0t):\psi_2(ta_2,-a_2s,a_1s-a_0t)],$$ and hence plugging $s=x_0a_2-a_0x_2$ and $t=x_1a_2-a_1x_2$ in to $(ta_2,-a_2s,a_1s-a_0t)$ gives $(a_2(x_1a_2-a_1x_2),-a_2(x_0a_2-a_0x_2),a_1x_0a_2-a_0x_1a_2)$, and factoring out the $a_2$ we get $(x_1a_2-a_1x_2,-(x_0a_2-a_0x_2),a_1x_0-a_0x_1)$, each component of which has bi-degree $(1,1)$. So we now have parametric equations for $C$, $$[x_0:x_1:x_2]=[\psi_0(v):\psi_1(v):\psi_2(v)],$$ where $v=(x_1a_2-a_1x_2,-x_0a_2+a_0x_2,a_1x_0-a_0x_1)$, so each component of the right hand side has bi-degree $(m,m+1)$. We get the following equations for $C$ (bi-homogeneous of degree $(m,m+2)$): $x_0\psi_1-x_1\psi_0=0$, $x_0\psi_2-x_2\psi_0=0$, $x_1\psi_2-x_2\psi_1=0$. The form $F^*(a,x)$ defining $C$ is a common divisor of these three equations. Thus $F^*$ is bi-homogeneous of bi-degree $(m',m+1)$ for some $m'\leq m$. Thus $F^*$ is bi-homogeneous of bi-degree $(m,m+1)$, and since it has a point of multiplicity at least $m$ at $a=x$ but degree exactly $m$, the multiplicity is also $m$.
nodes.statement_short: Implicit equations of bi-degree (m,m+2) force m'<=m, hence bi-degree (m,m+1) and multiplicity m.

nodes.name: Part (c)
nodes.statement:
(c) Since $F$ has degree $m$ in the $a$ variables, $F$ defines a curve of degree $m$ with a point of multiplicity $m$ at $a=x$, hence it defines a union of $m$ lines through the point $a=x$. The question remains as to what these lines are. To answer this question, translate the point $a=x$ to the point $[1:0:0]$. Doing this gives us $$G(a)=a_0^mF ig(1, rac{a_1}{a_0}+ rac{x_1}{x_0}, rac{a_2}{a_0}+ rac{x_2}{x_0},1, rac{x_1}{x_0}, rac{x_2}{x_0} ig) \in\ensuremath{\mathbb{K}}\Big[ rac{x_1}{x_0}, rac{x_2}{x_0}\Big][a_0,a_1,a_2].$$ In the $a$ variables, this defines $m$ lines meeting at $[1:0:0]$. Thus in the $a$ variables $G(a)$ is a homogeneous form of degree $m$, but now the variable $a_0$, which we can regard as defining the line at infinity, does not appear. Note that neither $a_1$ nor $a_2$ is a factor of $G(a)$, since if, say $a_1$ were a factor of $G$, then for all choices of $x$, $G=0$ includes the line from $[1:0:0]$ to $[0:0:1]$. Since the point $[0:0:1]$ is at infinity, it is fixed under the translation we employed, so $F(a_0,a_1,a_2,x_0,x_1,x_2)=0$ includes the line from $[x_0:x_1:x_2]$ to $[0:0:1]$, hence $x_1a_0-x_0a_1$ is a factor of $F$, contradicting the assumption that $C$ is irreducible. Since $a_0$ does not appear in $G(a)$ and $a_1$ and $a_2$ are not factors, we have $G(a)=b_0a_1^m+\cdots+b_ma_2^m$ with $b_i\in\ensuremath{\mathbb{K}} ig[ rac{x_1}{x_0}, rac{x_1}{x_0} ig]$ and $b_0,b_m
eq0$. Setting $a_2=1$ in $G$ gives $g(a_1)=b_0a_1^m+\cdots+b_m$ and dividing by $b_0$ gives $h(a_1)=g(a_1)/b_0\in\ensuremath{\mathbb{K}}( rac{x_1}{x_0}, rac{x_1}{x_0})[a_1]$. Over an appropriate field extension of $\ensuremath{\mathbb{K}}( rac{x_1}{x_0}, rac{x_1}{x_0})$ this factors as $h(a_1)=(a_1-h_1)\cdots(a_1-h_m)$. Note that the elements $h_i$ are distinct. If not, then $h$ and hence $g$ has a multiple root, say $h_i$, hence $a_1-h_i$ is a common factor of $g$ and $g'$ (or, taking more derivatives, of $g^{(\mu-1)}$ and $g^{(\mu)}$ if the root has multiplicity $\mu>1$) and thus can be found using the Euclidean algorithm. Thus the linear factor $a_1-h_i$ is in $\ensuremath{\mathbb{K}}( rac{x_1}{x_0}, rac{x_1}{x_0})[a_1]$ and so divides $g$ over $\ensuremath{\mathbb{K}}( rac{x_1}{x_0}, rac{x_1}{x_0})[a_1]$ and hence $a_1-h_ia_2$ divides $G(a)$ in $\ensuremath{\mathbb{K}} ig[ rac{x_1}{x_0}, rac{x_1}{x_0} ig][a_0,a_1,a_2]$ and thus $F(a,x)$ as before has a corresponding factor linear in $a$, contrary to assumption. Thus the roots $h_i$ are distinct. Since by Lemma ef{diffMap} the mapping $f$ expressing the coefficients of $h$ as symmetric functions of the roots $h_i$ has an invertible differential $df$ (the roots being distinct), we can by the inverse function theorem \cite[p.\ 33]{FG} regard the roots $h_i$ as holomorphic functions of the coefficients $b_i/b_0$ of $h$. Since each $b_i/b_0$ is a rational (and so holomorphic) function of $x_1/x_0$ and $x_2/x_0$, we can regard the $h_i$ as holomorphic functions of $x_1/x_0$ and $x_2/x_0$. The roots $h_i$ give the points at infinity where $G(a,x)$ vanishes. Specifically these are $[0:h_i:1]$. These are unaffected by affine translations, so the points where $F(a,x)$ vanishes on $a_0=0$ are these same points $[0:h_i:1]$. Thus translating back we see $F(a,x)$ vanishes on the lines through $[x_0:x_1:x_2]$ and $[0:h_i:1]$, so the forms defining these lines divide $F(a,x)$. Specifically, we have $G(a)=b_0(a_1-h_1a_2)\cdots(a_1-h_ma_2)$ so $$b_0\Big( rac{a_1}{a_0}-h_1 rac{a_2}{a_0}\Big)\cdots\Big( rac{a_1}{a_0}-h_m rac{a_2}{a_0}\Big)=G(a)/a_0^m= F\Big(1, rac{a_1}{a_0}+ rac{x_1}{x_0}, rac{a_2}{a_0}+ rac{x_2}{x_0},1, rac{x_1}{x_0}, rac{x_2}{x_0}\Big)$$ translates back to $$F(a,x)=x_0^{m+1}a_0^mb_0\Big( rac{a_1}{a_0}- rac{x_1}{x_0}- ig( rac{a_2}{a_0}- rac{x_2}{x_0} ig)h_1\Big)\cdots \Big( rac{a_1}{a_0}- rac{x_1}{x_0}- ig( rac{a_2}{a_0}- rac{x_2}{x_0} ig)h_m\Big)=$$ $$x_0b_0 ig((a_1x_0-a_0x_1)-(a_2x_0-a_0x_2)h_1 ig)\cdots  ig((a_1x_0-a_0x_1)-(a_2x_0-a_0x_2)h_m ig)=$$ $$b_0x_0\left| egin{array} {ccc} 0 & h_1(x) & 1\ x_0 & x_1 & x_2\ a_0 & a_1 & a_2\ \end{array} ight|\cdots \left| egin{array} {ccc} 0 & h_m(x) & 1\ x_0 & x_1 & x_2\ a_0 & a_1 & a_2\ \end{array} ight|.$$ Consider a point $x=a$ where $b_0x_0
eq0$. Then the branches of $F(a,x)=0$ in a neighborhood of $x=a$ are defined by the vanishing of each factor $\lambda_i(x_0,x_1,x_2)=\left| egin{array} {ccc} 0 & h_i(x) & 1\ x_0 & x_1 & x_2\ a_0 & a_1 & a_2\ \end{array} ight|$. The tangent line to the branch $\lambda_i(x)=0$ at $x=a$ is defined by $((
abla \lambda_i)|_{x=a})\cdot (x_0,x_1,x_2)$. Since $\lambda_i=(a_1-a_2h_i)x_0-a_0x_1+a_0x_2h_i$, the gradient $
abla \lambda_i$ is $$\Big((a_1-a_2h_i),-a_0,a_0h_i\Big)+\Big(-a_2h_{i0}x_0+a_0x_2h_{i0},-a_2h_{i1}x_0+a_0x_2h_{i1},-a_2h_{i2}x_0+a_0x_2h_{i2}\Big).$$ The second term vanishes at $x=a$ so $$(
abla \lambda_i)|_{x=a}\cdot(x_0,x_1,x_2)=(a_1-a_2h_i(x),-a_0,a_0h_i(x))|_{x=a}\cdot(x_0,x_1,x_2)=\left| egin{array} {ccc} 0 & h_i(a) & 1\ x_0 & x_1 & x_2\ a_0 & a_1 & a_2\ \end{array} ight|.$$ So we see that the tangent cone to $F(a,x)=0$ at a point $P=a$ such that $b_0x_0
eq0$ is defined by the vanishing of $$F_P(a,x)=b_0(a)a_0\left| egin{array} {ccc} 0 & h_1(a) & 1\ x_0 & x_1 & x_2\ a_0 & a_1 & a_2\ \end{array} ight|\cdots \left| egin{array} {ccc} 0 & h_m(a) & 1\ x_0 & x_1 & x_2\ a_0 & a_1 & a_2\ \end{array} ight|=$$ $$(-1)^mb_0(a)a_0\left| egin{array} {ccc} 0 & h_1(a) & 1\ a_0 & a_1 & a_2\ x_0 & x_1 & x_2\ \end{array} ight|\cdots \left| egin{array} {ccc} 0 & h_m(a) & 1\ a_0 & a_1 & a_2\ x_0 & x_1 & x_2\ \end{array} ight|=(-1)^mF(x,a).$$
nodes.statement_short: Identify the m lines in the a variables with the tangent lines to the branches.

nodes.name: m lines through a=x
nodes.statement: (c) Since $F$ has degree $m$ in the $a$ variables, $F$ defines a curve of degree $m$ with a point of multiplicity $m$ at $a=x$, hence it defines a union of $m$ lines through the point $a=x$.
nodes.statement_short: In a, F is m lines through a=x.

nodes.name: Translate to [1:0:0]
nodes.statement: The question remains as to what these lines are. To answer this question, translate the point $a=x$ to the point $[1:0:0]$. Doing this gives us $$G(a)=a_0^mF\big(1,\frac{a_1}{a_0}+\frac{x_1}{x_0},\frac{a_2}{a_0}+\frac{x_2}{x_0},1,\frac{x_1}{x_0},\frac{x_2}{x_0}\big) \in\ensuremath{\mathbb{K}}\Big[\frac{x_1}{x_0},\frac{x_2}{x_0}\Big][a_0,a_1,a_2].$$ In the $a$ variables, this defines $m$ lines meeting at $[1:0:0]$. Thus in the $a$ variables $G(a)$ is a homogeneous form of degree $m$, but now the variable $a_0$, which we can regard as defining the line at infinity, does not appear. Note that neither $a_1$ nor $a_2$ is a factor of $G(a)$, since if, say $a_1$ were a factor of $G$, then for all choices of $x$, $G=0$ includes the line from $[1:0:0]$ to $[0:0:1]$. Since the point $[0:0:1]$ is at infinity, it is fixed under the translation we employed, so $F(a_0,a_1,a_2,x_0,x_1,x_2)=0$ includes the line from $[x_0:x_1:x_2]$ to $[0:0:1]$, hence $x_1a_0-x_0a_1$ is a factor of $F$, contradicting the assumption that $C$ is irreducible.
nodes.statement_short: Translate a=x to [1:0:0]; a_1, a_2 are not factors since C is irreducible.

nodes.name: Distinct roots
nodes.statement: Since $a_0$ does not appear in $G(a)$ and $a_1$ and $a_2$ are not factors, we have $G(a)=b_0a_1^m+\cdots+b_ma_2^m$ with $b_i\in\ensuremath{\mathbb{K}}\big[\frac{x_1}{x_0},\frac{x_1}{x_0}\big]$ and $b_0,b_m\neq0$. Setting $a_2=1$ in $G$ gives $g(a_1)=b_0a_1^m+\cdots+b_m$ and dividing by $b_0$ gives $h(a_1)=g(a_1)/b_0\in\ensuremath{\mathbb{K}}(\frac{x_1}{x_0},\frac{x_1}{x_0})[a_1]$. Over an appropriate field extension of $\ensuremath{\mathbb{K}}(\frac{x_1}{x_0},\frac{x_1}{x_0})$ this factors as $h(a_1)=(a_1-h_1)\cdots(a_1-h_m)$. Note that the elements $h_i$ are distinct. If not, then $h$ and hence $g$ has a multiple root, say $h_i$, hence $a_1-h_i$ is a common factor of $g$ and $g'$ (or, taking more derivatives, of $g^{(\mu-1)}$ and $g^{(\mu)}$ if the root has multiplicity $\mu>1$) and thus can be found using the Euclidean algorithm. Thus the linear factor $a_1-h_i$ is in $\ensuremath{\mathbb{K}}(\frac{x_1}{x_0},\frac{x_1}{x_0})[a_1]$ and so divides $g$ over $\ensuremath{\mathbb{K}}(\frac{x_1}{x_0},\frac{x_1}{x_0})[a_1]$ and hence $a_1-h_ia_2$ divides $G(a)$ in $\ensuremath{\mathbb{K}}\big[\frac{x_1}{x_0},\frac{x_1}{x_0}\big][a_0,a_1,a_2]$ and thus $F(a,x)$ as before has a corresponding factor linear in $a$, contrary to assumption. Thus the roots $h_i$ are distinct.
nodes.statement_short: The roots h_i of the dehomogenized G are distinct, else F would have a factor linear in a.

nodes.name: Holomorphic roots
nodes.statement: Since by Lemma \ref{diffMap} the mapping $f$ expressing the coefficients of $h$ as symmetric functions of the roots $h_i$ has an invertible differential $df$ (the roots being distinct), we can by the inverse function theorem \cite[p.\ 33]{FG} regard the roots $h_i$ as holomorphic functions of the coefficients $b_i/b_0$ of $h$. Since each $b_i/b_0$ is a rational (and so holomorphic) function of $x_1/x_0$ and $x_2/x_0$, we can regard the $h_i$ as holomorphic functions of $x_1/x_0$ and $x_2/x_0$.
nodes.statement_short: Lemma 4.3 and the inverse function theorem make h_i holomorphic in x.

nodes.name: Factor F
nodes.statement: The roots $h_i$ give the points at infinity where $G(a,x)$ vanishes. Specifically these are $[0:h_i:1]$. These are unaffected by affine translations, so the points where $F(a,x)$ vanishes on $a_0=0$ are these same points $[0:h_i:1]$. Thus translating back we see $F(a,x)$ vanishes on the lines through $[x_0:x_1:x_2]$ and $[0:h_i:1]$, so the forms defining these lines divide $F(a,x)$. Specifically, we have $G(a)=b_0(a_1-h_1a_2)\cdots(a_1-h_ma_2)$ so $$b_0\Big(\frac{a_1}{a_0}-h_1\frac{a_2}{a_0}\Big)\cdots\Big(\frac{a_1}{a_0}-h_m\frac{a_2}{a_0}\Big)=G(a)/a_0^m= F\Big(1,\frac{a_1}{a_0}+\frac{x_1}{x_0},\frac{a_2}{a_0}+\frac{x_2}{x_0},1,\frac{x_1}{x_0},\frac{x_2}{x_0}\Big)$$ translates back to $$F(a,x)=x_0^{m+1}a_0^mb_0\Big(\frac{a_1}{a_0}-\frac{x_1}{x_0}-\big(\frac{a_2}{a_0}-\frac{x_2}{x_0}\big)h_1\Big)\cdots \Big(\frac{a_1}{a_0}-\frac{x_1}{x_0}-\big(\frac{a_2}{a_0}-\frac{x_2}{x_0}\big)h_m\Big)=$$ $$x_0b_0\big((a_1x_0-a_0x_1)-(a_2x_0-a_0x_2)h_1\big)\cdots \big((a_1x_0-a_0x_1)-(a_2x_0-a_0x_2)h_m\big)=$$ $$b_0x_0\left|\begin{array} {ccc} 0 & h_1(x) & 1\\ x_0 & x_1 & x_2\\ a_0 & a_1 & a_2\\ \end{array} \right|\cdots \left|\begin{array} {ccc} 0 & h_m(x) & 1\\ x_0 & x_1 & x_2\\ a_0 & a_1 & a_2\\ \end{array} \right|.$$
nodes.statement_short: F(a,x) factors as a product of determinants through [0:h_i:1].

nodes.name: Tangent lines of branches
nodes.statement:
Consider a point $x=a$ where $b_0x_0
eq0$. Then the branches of $F(a,x)=0$ in a neighborhood of $x=a$ are defined by the vanishing of each factor $\lambda_i(x_0,x_1,x_2)=\left| egin{array} {ccc} 0 & h_i(x) & 1\ x_0 & x_1 & x_2\ a_0 & a_1 & a_2\ \end{array} ight|$. The tangent line to the branch $\lambda_i(x)=0$ at $x=a$ is defined by $((
abla \lambda_i)|_{x=a})\cdot (x_0,x_1,x_2)$. Since $\lambda_i=(a_1-a_2h_i)x_0-a_0x_1+a_0x_2h_i$, the gradient $
abla \lambda_i$ is $$\Big((a_1-a_2h_i),-a_0,a_0h_i\Big)+\Big(-a_2h_{i0}x_0+a_0x_2h_{i0},-a_2h_{i1}x_0+a_0x_2h_{i1},-a_2h_{i2}x_0+a_0x_2h_{i2}\Big).$$ The second term vanishes at $x=a$ so $$(
abla \lambda_i)|_{x=a}\cdot(x_0,x_1,x_2)=(a_1-a_2h_i(x),-a_0,a_0h_i(x))|_{x=a}\cdot(x_0,x_1,x_2)=\left| egin{array} {ccc} 0 & h_i(a) & 1\ x_0 & x_1 & x_2\ a_0 & a_1 & a_2\ \end{array} ight|.$$
nodes.statement_short: Compute the gradient of each branch at x=a.

nodes.name: Tangent cone is F(x,a)
nodes.statement: So we see that the tangent cone to $F(a,x)=0$ at a point $P=a$ such that $b_0x_0\neq0$ is defined by the vanishing of $$F_P(a,x)=b_0(a)a_0\left|\begin{array} {ccc} 0 & h_1(a) & 1\\ x_0 & x_1 & x_2\\ a_0 & a_1 & a_2\\ \end{array} \right|\cdots \left|\begin{array} {ccc} 0 & h_m(a) & 1\\ x_0 & x_1 & x_2\\ a_0 & a_1 & a_2\\ \end{array} \right|=$$ $$(-1)^mb_0(a)a_0\left|\begin{array} {ccc} 0 & h_1(a) & 1\\ a_0 & a_1 & a_2\\ x_0 & x_1 & x_2\\ \end{array} \right|\cdots \left|\begin{array} {ccc} 0 & h_m(a) & 1\\ a_0 & a_1 & a_2\\ x_0 & x_1 & x_2\\ \end{array} \right|=(-1)^mF(x,a).$$
nodes.statement_short: The tangent cone at P equals (-1)^m F(x,a).

nodes.name: CHMN decomposition
nodes.statement: It is shown in \cite{CHMN} that $C=C'\cup \Lambda_1\cup\cdots\cup \Lambda_r$ where $C'$ is unexpected for a subset $Z'$ of $Z$ and has degree $m+1-r$ with a general point $P$ of multiplicity $m-r$ where $r=|Z|-|Z'|$ and each $\Lambda_i$ is the line from $P$ to $p_i$ where $p_1,\ldots, p_r$ are the points of $Z$ not in $Z'$.
nodes.statement_short: C is an irreducible unexpected curve C' plus lines through P.

nodes.name: Factor F
nodes.statement: Thus $F=GL_1\cdots L_r$, where $G$ is the form defining $C'$ and $L_i$ is the bi-linear form defining $\Lambda_i$.

nodes.name: Antisymmetry of line factors
nodes.statement: So we have $F^*=G^*L_1^*\cdots L_r^*$, but $L_i^*=L_i$ and $L_i(a,x)=-L_(x,a)$, so $F^*(a,x)=(G^*L_1\cdots L_r)(a,x)=(-1)^m(G^*L_1\cdots L_r)(x,a)$.
nodes.statement_short: Each L_i is antisymmetric, giving the sign (-1)^m.

nodes.name: Combine tangent cones
nodes.statement: The tangent cone for $C$ is the tangent cone for $C'$ union with the lines $L_i$, so we also see that $(-1)^mG^*(x,a)L_1^*(x,a)\cdots L_r^*(x,a)=F^*(x,a)$ defines the tangent cone for $C$.
nodes.statement_short: Tangent cone of C is that of C' union the lines.
